Wow! I’m addicted to McFadden’s writing—her unpredictable, mind-blowing twists, brilliant sense of humor, and fast-paced, short chapters that keep me hooked! I love her books! I know reading is subjective—you don’t have to like her characters or may even find them naive, questioning their intelligence with harsh adjectives. Honestly, I don’t care! For me, I enjoy the inner thoughts of her seemingly naive characters, which often make me laugh because of the sarcasm and dark humor in their thoughts and actions. (Criticizing heroines for panicking and making mistakes is like questioning why blonde women in horror movies always die first or how the 'final girl' manages to survive, even if she’s not a genius!) The story revolves around Sydney, a 34-year-old accountant living in a nice New York apartment. Recently heartbroken after her breakup with her detective boyfriend Jake, Sydney’s financial situation doesn't match her unlucky love life. She dives into the dating pool through a popular app, but her recent dates have been disastrous. Her last date, Kevin, even attempted to assault her on the street, turning into a stalkerish nightmare. Thankfully, she’s saved by a mysterious stranger that night, but she doesn't hear from them again—until fate brings them together after her best friend, who lived in her apartment, is brutally murdered. We also get flashbacks of Tom’s past, though his identity isn’t revealed immediately. Tom, a nice and sweet high school boy, befriends an awkward outcast nicknamed Slug, and falls in love with Daisy, the police chief's daughter. But Tom’s darker instincts slowly drag him into a whirlwind of tragedies, including the deaths of young women in his neighborhood. How will Sydney and Tom’s paths cross? Has Sydney unknowingly invited danger into her life? If you want to know more, hop on McFadden’s fright train and read this in one sitting! It’s guaranteed fun, as always. McFadden’s thrill rides never disappoint! Anyway, I enjoyed this book! Interestingly, I even enjoyed the flashbacks to Tom’s story. I found Sydney, the main heroine, tolerable, especially since I laughed out loud every time her mother called with awkward reminders about her biological clock ticking! The smart twist left me speechless—even the sharpest reader wouldn’t see it coming. I also enjoyed the ending! The pacing was great, as usual, and the way Sydney’s present-day POV intertwined with Tom’s past was surprisingly well done. Overall: I’m giving this 4 stars! It is always a book treat to read a Nicholas Sparks novel and I’m happy to report that this was another fine read by the global bestselling author. Told over seven page turning parts and sixty-eight engrossing chapters, Dreamland is the twenty fourth release from Nicholas Sparks, an author who needs no introduction. Utilising an alternating form of narration between a man named Colby and a woman named Beverly, Sparks presents two vastly different viewpoints. It is hard to see how and when Sparks will make the character linkage, but I placed my complete trust in one of my favourite writers. Dreamland features a very immersive narrative style which allowed me to develop a lasting bond with Beverly. Sparks really involves the reader in Beverly’s narrative, so we feel an overwhelming sense of urgency, despair, nervousness and fear. She was secretive and appeared to be very nervous and frightened. Jeri believed that one of the sitting judges in Lacy’s jurisdiction was a serial killer. Could Jeri convince Lacy to help her prove that this sitting judge committed several murders while acting as a judge in the state of Florida? The Judge’s List by John Grisham was fast paced and kept me guessing throughout the book. The characters were colorful and complex. With intuition and detective skills that would rightfully embarrass the FBI and any number of municipal police departments, Crosby has accumulated a barrel full of circumstantial evidence suggesting that a well-respected, practicing Florida judge is a relentlessly patient, ruthless, sociopathic, and very skilled serial murderer with over 10 kill notches on his gavel. It has been one of my annual late Fall rituals. The leaves are falling. School is back in, College and Pro football are in high gear, and it’s time to open the new John Grisham novel, “The Judge’s List”, and re-visit the law in action through the eyes of a challenged do-gooder. This time out, Grisham changes it up a bit. Although this new book involves some aspects of the law and legal issues, it is more of a Michael Connelly or David Baldacci crime thriller, written with that unique Grisham storytelling touch. “The Judge’s List” re-introduces us to Lacy Stolz, an investigator for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct (BJC). Her job is to respond to any complaints dealing with ethical or judicial misconduct by members of the court. Lacy was one of the protagonists in his previous 2016 legal Thriller, “The Whistler”, investigating a corrupt Florida judge who was taking bribes from a major crime syndicate. Although she helped catch the judge and members of the syndicate, her partner killed, and she barely survived being attacked herself. Now, three years later and closing in on the age of forty, she is still working for the BJC and waiting for her big legal claim against the syndicate to settle so she can move on to better things. Then things change when Lacy gets an anonymous call from an unknown woman. Not just any woman, but one who is so scared she is using burner phones, multiple aliases, and unbelievably paranoid. After agreeing to meet with her several times, Lacy learns that the woman’s name is Jeri Crosby and she has an incredible story, that if true, will rock the sanctity of the Florida legal system. Jeri has been stalking a man for twenty years that she passionately believes is a cold-blooded serial killer, who kills those that have angered him in some way. It doesn’t matter how serious or minor the reason. The killer is patient, willing to wait to more than a decade to seek revenge on those who angered him. His pattern of murder and weapons used is the same every time and Jeri has been obsessive in her research of his relationships to every victim, which adds up to at least seven or eight victims that she is aware of. But she knows there are probably more, because her father was the potential third victim, and that started on this journey that she cannot stop until he is stopped. And to make the situation more complicated… According to Jeri, the killer is a Florida judge, under the jurisdiction of Lacy’s own BJC. Because Jeri distrusts the police, and even the FBI, she files a complaint to the BJC through Lacy, thinking that will protect herself. The good news is that she has motive and intent, but the bad news is that she has no hard evidence or proof. Everything is circumstantial. And what Jeri and Lacy don’t know is that the killer is an expert not only in the law, but also in investigations, forensics, evidence, and not leaving a trail. He’s constantly one step ahead of law enforcement and now he is setting his deadly sights on Jeri and Lacy… Over the last several years, it seemed to me that Grisham was shifting his writing from pure legal thrillers to more plots addressing his personal feelings of injustice within the American legal system. His themes have been more aimed on exposing serious societal issues like the death penalty, wrongful convictions, race inequality, and how the law can be abused by those in positions of power. Grisham is definitely an advocate of the underprivileged and mistreated, and well, this book allows him a large soapbox to stand on and deliver both a legal drama combined together with resolving the inequalities of an imperfect legal system. However, this time he has chosen to branch out and try his hand at writing a crime thriller rather than a courtroom-centered legal drama. He doesn’t do too bad, primarily for two big reasons. One, his premise and set-up is enticing and good. The plot is interesting and pulls you in easily and fast like most of his books do. The second reason is that his writing style is just so dang good. Grisham is a master writer and his writing style just demands your attention is such a fluid and effortless manner. His descriptions are brief, focused, and vivid. His dialogs are sharp and flow like a Robert B. Parker Spenser novel at its best. More importantly. Like Stephen King, Grisham is a pure in heart storyteller, and his storytelling skills are pretty flawless – smooth and flowing prose with no wasted or unnecessary words, a constant focus on moving the conflict forward. Now, that doesn’t mean there was not some areas where the book could have been better. There were some weaknesses, most of which come from stepping into a different genre. For example, it took Lacy a long time to be drawn into Jeri’s situation and it never felt like she was really ever fully invested in the investigation. Also, you could see where Jeri was headed in the storyline pretty fast, and the way she acted at times made her less sympathetic. I wanted to like her more, but I struggled at times more than I wanted to because of her being so overly protective one moment and then so outrageously stupid the next moment. I know it was because Grisham needed her to interject twists and turns into the storyline, but sometimes I wanted to say, seriously dude! Stop it. I guess my biggest complaint (and it is not a major one) is that her silly behaviors were what provided the most conflict and suspense into the storyline. I also found myself conflicted by the ending. I need to be careful here and not give anything away for those who haven’t read it yet, so I will tread lightly. I know that Grisham was trying to surprise his readers with an unexpected outcome, but I am not sure he stuck the landing. I’ve been thinking pretty hard for the last 24 hours about how I felt about it and I am still feeling less than satisfied with the overall outcome. Enough to deduct a half star for it, even if it puts me in the minority of most readers. Sorry, but that’s my current state of mind. Overall, this was still a pretty enjoyable and entertaining book, another of his usual page-turners from beginning to almost the end. Although it wasn’t stretching too far from his home turf, it turned out to be a safe risk that turned out pretty well. Let’s face it. Grisham sets such a high bar that sometimes it’s hard to review his work with full objectively, since beauty is in the eyes of the beholder. I believe that that the key to Grisham’s continued success is his exemplary power to tell a captivating tale and this one was, although not one his absolute best novels, was still one that checked enough of the reader’s boxes (story, characters, and setting) for me. My rating – 3.5 out of 5 stars. See you again next year, John…

As a fan of the Harry Bosch series, I enjoyed Connelly's latest police procedural story. Renee Ballard is the main character, and she works The Dark Hours, meaning the midnight shift. She enlists retired cop, now private detective, Harry Bosch, to help her solve the two crimes she's investigating. Ballard is a loner, a surfer, and a good cop, but she doesn't always let department policy get in the way of finding the bad guys. She has a few narrow escapes, plus a new love interest. She also adopts a puppy, Pinto, a cute chihuahua mix. I didn't like a lot of the police jargon but it provided authenticity, a trademark of the Bosch series.

This is the twenty-third book in the Harry Bosch series, however, in the last few, Renee Ballard, a young female detective, has been taking a greater role—this is the fourth book with her in a major role. In all but one of these she is partnered with Bosch. She was first introduced in the 2007 book The Overlook. In this book she is the lead and Bosch is only a minor supporting character. Ballard is a feminine clone of Bosch. She likes working alone and she is almost constantly in conflict with her superiors. This mystery involves a couple of serial rapists, but while tracking them Ballard is called to the scene of a murder. When the department heads try to hand off the murder case to another department Ballard continues her investigation hoping to solve the case before the handoff while simultaneously working the rapist case. This two case story line seems to be popular with the Bosch books of late. I don’t remember the earlier books having that type of story line. This story occurs at the beginning of 2021 and includes several references to some of the happenings of the time. There are several comments about these circumstances by Bosch, Ballard and others. The “Defund the Police” idea is described as having a detrimental effect on the police department. It is said that the police have become reactive instead of proactive. They want no unnecessary interaction with the public. When Ballard mentions that she is thinking of leaving the police force, Bosch points out that true reform must come from inside the police department and she should stay and become part of that reform. There is also mention of the importance of wearing a mask due to the Covid pandemic. But in another eery coincidence as I write this on the anniversary of the Jan. 6th insurrection, Bosch and others express their shock at the Capitol being invaded by Americans when that event occurs during the story. I doubt if many readers pick up a mystery like any of Michael Connelly’s books expecting some social commentary. The fact that I agree with many of these views does not negate the distractions they brought to the story. At the end of the book Ballard has resigned from the police department, but there are hints that she will return. She is an interesting addition to the mystery genre and I will look forward to the next book by Michael Connelly hoping he continues her story.

The pandemic is in full swing in Los Angeles and much of the force is burned out. But LAPD Detective Renée Ballard is not letting herself be one of those officers. In fact, she's picking up the slack of her fellow coworkers. Ballard is working a rapist case deemed the "Midnight Men," whose lead seems like she could care less about the case or the female victims. And New Year's brings Ballard the shooting of a former gang member. While she should pass the murder on to homicide, Ballard tries to work it as long as possible when she realizes the shooting is linked to a cold case of Harry Bosch's. As Bosch and Ballard team up again, they start to realize where their cases intersect. And as they do, they come on the radar of a killer who would much prefer to stay hidden. "She knew this could be the solve she needed to save herself." Harry Bosch will forever be my one true love. I love him dearly and always will. Ballard is definitely growing on me, and I really respected her in this book. This is a really timely read, as Connelly does not shy away from the pandemic, riots, anger toward the police, and police apathy and burnout. As always, we get his superb knowledge of police procedures, excellent research, and two wonderful investigators in Bosch and Ballard. I've never watched the Bosch show, but I feel like I can picture Bosch and Ballard so clearly due to Connelly's wonderful writing and world building. THE DARK HOURS finds Ballard in a tough place. She may love doing the actual police work, but she does have growing disillusion with her job, department, and the people. But, as she says, Bosch is her true constant. (I feel you, Renee, he's mine too!) She's going through a lot and always fighting an uphill battle against the jerks who seem against her at every turn. But Ballard is tough--much like a certain Harry Bosch--and watching the two of them solve cases is pure joy. Both cases presented in HOURS are complex and interesting, especially the New Year's shooting of Ballard's that links to Bosch's cold case. The two zig and zag around L.A., making connections and generally keeping us on our toes. It's wonderful having their two minds together. Overall, this is another great mystery, featuring two excellent characters, and since the ending leaves us hanging a bit, I look forward to another book. 4+ stars. Too Late by Colleen Hoover ⭐️⭐️⭐️ (3.75 stars) Tropes & Themes: 🚩 Toxic love triangle 🖤 Obsession vs. real love 😵‍💫 Morally grey everything 🚨 Dark romance 👮‍♂️ Undercover cop 💔 Coercive control 🔥 Taboo spice 🏃‍♀️ Escape from danger ⸻ So I finally read Too Late after hearing people rave about how “different” it is from Colleen Hoover’s usual stuff, and wow… yeah, they weren’t kidding. 😬 This book is wild, disturbing, and honestly felt like I was reading someone’s fever dream at times BUT in a way I couldn’t stop reading?? The story follows Sloan, a college student who’s basically trapped in a toxic, controlling relationship with Asa, a powerful drug dealer. She’s stuck because of financial reasons and because he literally won’t let her leave. And honestly, Asa is one of the most terrifying fictional characters I’ve ever read like, textbook narcissist, emotionally manipulative, and extremely dangerous. 🚩🚩🚩 Then we meet Carter (aka undercover cop Luke), who moves into Asa’s circle to bring down his operation… but ends up falling for Sloan along the way. Cue the forbidden love, undercover mission, and emotional whiplash from all the things that go down. It’s basically Netflix thriller meets Wattpad fanfic 😅 ⸻ What I liked: ✅ The pace was quick and addictive. I couldn’t put it down even when it made me uncomfortable ✅ Carter (or Luke?) was a breath of fresh air and gave me the “quiet, protective, respectful guy” vibes I love ✅ I appreciated that CoHo didn’t romanticize Asa at all, he’s truly evil and that’s made very clear ✅ The rawness and chaos of the story kept me engaged, even when I didn’t like it ⸻ What I didn’t like: 🚨 This book is DARK. Like, trigger warnings galore dark (SA, abuse, manipulation, drugs, etc.) 📝 The writing felt unpolished more like something she wrote for fun and decided to release later (which I think she did?) 😬 Some of the spicy scenes were straight up uncomfortable and felt unnecessary 🧠 I felt emotionally drained after reading it tbh 🤷‍♀️ The plot got a bit ridiculous toward the end and felt rushed/wrapped up too neatly considering how serious everything was ⸻ Overall Thoughts: This definitely isn’t for everyone and if you’re not in the right headspace, I’d say skip it. It’s raw, disturbing, and feels more like CoHo’s experimental “what-if-I-just-went-feral” book than a traditional romance. But if you’re in the mood for something dark, messy, and morally complex, it will keep you turning the pages. ⸻ Rating: 3.75 stars 📖 Addictive, dark, and deeply unsettling 🖤 Not romantic in the traditional sense, but compelling in a car-crash-you-can’t-look-away-from way 😵‍💫 For fans of chaotic drama and unhinged vibes Would I recommend it? This one is my favorite book in the Never After series so far. McIntire truly outdid herself with this dark, twisted Little Mermaid retelling. Venesa is one of the strongest, most compelling FMCs in the entire series, cold, intelligent, morally grey, and shaped by trauma in a way that feels raw and believable. I loved watching her step into her power instead of softening for love. Enzo was the perfect match for her: dangerous, loyal, and emotionally layered. Their chemistry was intense, forbidden, and slow-burning in the best way. The romance felt earned, not rushed, and I appreciated that neither character had to lose their darkness to be together. The mafia setting worked incredibly well, adding high stakes, tension, and violence that enhanced the story rather than overshadowing the romance. The Little Mermaid parallels, especially the symbolism surrounding voice, sacrifice, and control, were subtle but clever. At the beginning, I actually felt sympathy for Aria. Her instability and desperation made her feel tragic rather than purely villainous, which added an extra emotional layer to the story as her arc progressed. While the pacing dragged slightly in the middle, the payoff was absolutely worth it. The final act was ruthless, satisfying, and empowering. Also loved the epilogue!

— 4 stars 🐚🪸 ”you have changed me. irrevocably. i don’t want you in a different life. i need you in this one and all the ones we’ll have after.” enzo and venesa’s soundtrack ₊˚⊹🧪 hexed is the sixth installment in emily mcintire’s never after series, and my personal third read of the series. though it wasn’t quite a five star read for me, it still delivered an enjoyable, gripping story. this book was one of the more plot driven entries, offering a refreshing take with a female villain lead and weaving a compelling dynamic between forbidden love, loyalty, and betrayal. while not my favorite of the series, it sits comfortably between my thoughts on hooked and twisted, bringing both strengths and weaknesses from each. — plot: unlike the more atmospheric twisted, hexed was very much plot driven, and for the most part, it worked. the story was fleshed out, characters outside the main couple were given meaningful roles, and the forbidden aspect of their relationship tied in nicely with the larger narrative. i appreciated how mcIntire took her time building the world and weaving the subplots into the main storyline. — venesa was easily the highlight of hexed. she’s dynamic, complex, and the perfect embodiment of a morally grey female villain. what stood out was how round her character felt; she had depth, clear motivations, and genuine development throughout the story. venesa wasn’t just a flat “bad girl” trope; she was layered, powerful, and driven by her own sense of justice and revenge. watching her navigate her ambitions while being forced to confront vulnerability gave her a strong arc that i genuinely appreciated. her character alone was enough to keep me invested. “you can't ever count on a man, but you can always count on the poison that will kill him... or whatever that saying is.” — enzo’s character development was enjoyable as well, especially in how his loyalties shifted over time. his internal struggle between duty and desire added much needed tension to the story. that said, while i liked him, i didn’t love him. compared to the soulmates level chemistry i felt with julian and yasmin in twisted, enzo and venesa’s dynamic didn’t hit quite as hard. their connection was compelling in a forbidden love, can’t have you way, but it lacked the slow burn build up and tension that really makes a romance hit emotionally. (even if the first smut scene was 300 pages in, they had feelings for each other very early on.) from the very start, they were drawn to each other, which worked for the plot, but didn’t leave much room for that slow burn angst. ”she's poise and grace in the face of adversity. polished on the outside. and it gives me a thrill to know she's capable of being so bad at the flip of a switch.” — romance and chemistry: this brings me to the romance: good, but not great. their chemistry was there, but it didn’t scream power couple energy. they felt more like two very broken people who found comfort and desire in each other rather than a destined, soulmate level match. and while that worked for the story, it didn’t give me the same level of emotional payoff as other couples in the series. think more “we understand each other’s darkness” than “fated lovers”. as a bridgerton season 2 lover, i appreciated the “i want you but i can’t have you” dynamic, and hexed definitely scratched that itch, but it still missed that extra spark that would’ve pushed it to a five star for me. — the pacing faltered at the climax. the final twists, especially the reveal of who killed who, felt brushed over too quickly. after so much build up, those pivotal moments lacked the weight and drama they deserved. the deaths toward the end, particularly in the first epilogue, felt anticlimactic. with characters who were hyped up to be so dangerous and untouchable, seeing them taken down in just a few pages was underwhelming. for a book that invested so much in creating tension, the payoff didn’t quite match the setup. -1 ★… i deducted one star because the romance lacked the emotional build up and tension i wanted, making venesa and enzo feel less like a power couple and more like two broken people who happened to fit. the final twists and character deaths felt rushed and anticlimactic, especially after so much build up. plus, the long break in my reading hurt my connection to the story, which dulled the overall impact. (i started this book in december, got 400 pages in, then never picked it up again until may bc school started back 😭.) ₊⊹⁀➴ in conclusion, hexed was an enjoyable read that kept my interest and made me want to continue the series. venesa’s character alone was worth the read, and the forbidden romance trope was done well enough to satisfy, even if it didn’t fully deliver that all consuming chemistry i love. the plot was engaging, even if the climax stumbled a bit, and the book’s sheer size allowed for more layered storytelling compared to earlier installments. it didn’t dethrone twisted as my favorite, but it absolutely sits above hooked. if you’re a fan of morally grey female leads, forbidden romance, and plot driven dark romance with a dash of bridgerton season two tension, you’ll enjoy this one. as for me, i’m cautiously eyeing scarred next, even if the fantasy element makes me a little nervous. and i’m STILL manifesting that princess and the frog inspired book from mcintire. give me new orleans and my tiana and dr. facilier dark romance PLEASEEEE. ➸ never after book 1 review ➸ never after book 4 review

It is always refreshing to read a new Brad Thor novel. With the passing of author Tom Clancy back in 2013 the literary world was left with a gaping hole of political thriller writers with a conservative sensibility. Thor has more than picked up the gauntlet and filled this void and his Scot Harvath series continues to make in impact with themes and stories that are an ideal fit for the world of political turmoil we all currently live in. BLACK ICE finds, at least initially, a far more mellow version of the Scot Harvath we have grown to love throughout this series. He has had to deal with a lot of change --- both in the political climate that has changed his role as a special agent as well as the personal loss of his friend and mentor with his organization, The Carlton Group. Readers of this series also understand that Harvath is an ex-Navy Seal and ex-Secret Service member who has a special set of skills that has found him in demand for projects few others could accomplish. First off, let’s break down the title of this novel and the significance the term plays throughout this novel. The rapidly melting sea ice in the Arctic Waters --- a Blue Arctic --- will create new opportunities and challenges for world powers that seek to exploit the area, specifically the United States, Russia, and China. Since the current value system of the U.S. vastly differs from those other two World Powers it will become imperative that we prevent them from using such natural resources to wrest power from our country. There is a great action sequence at the beginning of the novel where Harvath is in a helicopter with two other men that is about to crash in the very same Arctic territory. We will see this sequence in detail later in BLACK ICE --- and it’s one of the best action sequences I’ve read in a while --- but first we must go back 72 hours prior to this event to set up the plot. Scot Harvath is having a great summer in Oslo, Norway, with his true love, Solvi, and things could not be better since he stepped away from his previous line of work. That is until he literally sees a ghost, a man who Harvath had personally killed years earlier appearing before his eyes. America’s top spy is quickly called back into action in a race against not only time but also the combined efforts of China and Russia. He is brought up to speed on what those countries are plotting and it involves control of the Arctic Shelf and threats of nuclear power being utilized in that region. China is seen as the largest threat here, especially since the ‘ghost’ Harvath saw stepping from a taxi earlier was Colonel Jiang Shi of the People’s Liberation Army. A really bad guy with a lot of power who Harvath swore had been eliminated from the political chessboard. The race to get icebreaker ships into the Arctic has become a reality and it seems the U.S. is way behind in this area. Harvath turns things on and seems to run on automatic pilot in situations like this, an intelligent killing-machine who is willing to do anything to achieve the goals of his assignment. He relies upon his loyal band of colleagues that have been there for him throughout his super spy life, and it is great to see the old gang together again. China’s goal is to disrupt radar technology in a mission labelled “Black Ice” and Scot Harvath may be the only person standing between them and success. BLACK ICE is a slow burn of a novel that spends a lot of time establishing the players and the moves being made in this political game. However, once the last third of the novel kicks into gear we get to see Brad Thor at his best with action sequences that will literally chill readers while simultaneously taking their breath away. Scot Harvath is the only person for this job, and he is the hero we need to do whatever it takes to maintain our security and safety in the face of so much adversity in the form of our political rivals. Well, I'm actually hesitant about starting this review. First of all, let me say that Scot Harvath is one of my absolute favorite book characters. I have read and listened to every one of Brad Thor's books and have gone on all of the journeys alongside Scot. I have cried - especially just recently - when Scot lost absolutely everything and everyone that he loved. Yet, life does go on and I was happy that he was able to move forward and especially when he was able to met out his own form of justice. Okay, that is a long way of saying that I'm a fan, but I am also a reader. So why am I hesitant? The premise of this book was interesting. I can honestly say that I learn so much about geo-political relationships and strategic situations from Mr. Thor. He brings things to my attention and because I am curious by nature, afterwards I end up looking for more information on subjects that I am not familiar with so that I can be more informed. The fight for artic land and ship channels is one that I have been hearing about for the last couple of years and it was intriguing to have the book plot revolve around that. Unfortunately, for once, the plot of the story really wasn't front and center. I never thought I would complain about Scot's romantic life. So, I guess I should learn to stop saying never. To me, the relationship between Scot and Solvi seemed forced. And there was just so much emphasis on it that it ended up pulling me out of the story. Do I have a problem with Scot having a significant other? Absolutely not. But, honestly, his wife JUST died. I mean, seriously was murdered right in front of him. They were married less than a day and then his life exploded. So do I think it's a bit soon? Umm.....yes. But, in life, things happen so if he met someone that he was able to move forward with, okay. But then with what happened at the end of the book, that was a shocker. What in the world is the rush? So, that is one issue. The other thing that was different was that as I mentioned before, the plot itself seemed to take a back seat to other things. We get to meet a new character that supposedly was close with the "Old Man" and in order to hear about how he got his nickname we are told this really LONG and involved story that was interesting but again, it didn't quite fit into the flow of the storyline. Just superficial information. Then, Scot calls his "team" to join him in Norway but I'm not sure why. They really didn't end up doing anything. They didn't help him when he was in serious trouble.....either time. Nicholas provided some support, but he could have done that from anywhere. Again, pieces of things that normally fit very well together but for once, didn't fit. Does this mean that I didn't like the book? No. I did. Even a bad Brad Thor book is better than 90% of all other books. And it wasn't bad. It was just unexpected. I went back and forth between a 3 star and a 4 star rating and decided to go with 4. Mr. Thor has built up a heck of a lot of credibility with me. I listened to most of this on Audible and as usual, felt that Armand Schultz did a wonderful job. One thing though - it mentions that there is a bonus conversation with Brad and Armand at the end of the audio version. For whatever reason, my audio version did not have that. I would really have liked to hear the two of them talk about the series. Oh well. Now, it is time for the wait again. That awful time after the yearly book has been finished and we know that it is going to be another year until we get the next book. But, I will wait because as I said in the beginning, I am a fan.

I think I have my next thriller author. I liked how everything was tied up in a neat bundle.

A warrior believes in an end she can’t see and fights for it. A warrior never gives up. A warrior fights for those weaker than herself. It sounds like motherhood to me. Kristin Hannah's books seem to get pigeonholed as "women's fiction", whatever that means, but the three books I've read from her - The Nightingale, The Great Alone, and this one - have all been, for me, nothing short of survival stories. The theme of women surviving impossible times runs through all three of the books I've read by Hannah. She often focuses on cross-generational bonds, between older and younger women who usually have complex relationships with one another. The Nightingale focused on the women left fighting their own war at home in France during the German occupation. The Great Alone follows a mother and daughter into the Alaskan wilderness, as they fight off threats from outside and within their small cabin. The Four Winds is set during dust bowl era Texas, and focuses on Elsa Martinelli and her daughter as they try to survive the complete destruction of life as they knew it. You know, before reading this book, I thought I understood what happened during the dust bowl and the Great Depression. I read The Grapes of Wrath some years ago and we skimmed over it in school. But clearly I did not appreciate the horrors that took place, especially in the dust-ravaged lands of Northern Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico. I did not know, or did not remember, that people slept in gas masks or else woke with their eyes crusted shut and their throats caked in dirt. I did not know how many died from dust pneumonia. In this book, Elsa has carved out a piece of paradise for herself-- a loving family, a land to farm and be proud of, and a mother-in-law whose initial suspicion quickly turns to affection. Then the land turns on them. Everything dies. There's no food to feed themselves, never mind the few animals they need to keep their farm going. And then Elsa's son becomes gravely ill, and she must decide whether to stick it out and hope for an end to this hell, or leave on a perilous journey west to California. It's just a real great story about a family trying to survive. I loved Elsa immediately, her fire and her weaknesses, and I wanted so badly for her to get her family to safety. The trials never stop, though, and after doing a bit more outside reading on the dust bowl, I can see there was nothing remarkable about Elsa's story, even if, to me, it sounds completely outrageous. The Four Winds is not a short book, but I ate it up. I was so absorbed in the story that I felt annoyed every time real life disturbed my reading. This book just cemented Kristin Hannah as a must-read author for me.

Another Kristin Hannah book that absolutely ripped my heart out by the end 😍 idk why I expected different! Elsa marries into a family with a lot of land as the Great Depression & the Dust Bowl hits them hard. It’s super character driven with a very slow pacing plot (which is a reason it’s not rated higher), but I connected to Elsa early on! She goes through SO MUCH (as did so many people during this time) and proves through everything just how much she’d do for her children + how much bravery and strength she has. I love Kristin Hannah’s writing & following Elsa/learning more about this time through her perspective

This is America during the 1930’s. This is America after the stock market crash. This is America of the dust bowl. This is America of the forgotten farmer and the unemployed turned migrant worker: homeless, poverty stricken experiencing starvation, cruelty, and despair. This is a book that urges us to look back and lament. Given what is going on in my country this is an America perilously close to a precipitous edge. Let’s hope that these hard times don’t become the “worst hard times.”

The book tells the story of a girl named Elsa. When she first appears in the book, she seems as fragile as glass. She was well-protected by her family because the doctors said she was ill, leading to many restrictions in her life. At the age of 25, she suddenly breaks free from these restrictions. One day, she puts on a beautiful dress, goes out, meets an 18-year-old boy named Rafe, and has sex with him. This event changes Elsa because she becomes pregnant. There's a part of the story I don't quite understand: Elsa's parents, who had always been protective of her, abandon her upon learning about her pregnancy. They don’t even visit her after she has the baby, which seems incredibly heartless, making me question whether Elsa is their biological daughter. Fortunately, Elsa's in-laws treat her very well. As a mother, Elsa faces various challenges and proves to be much stronger than the doctors had suggested. What captivates me about this book is Elsa's struggle with life. She faces numerous hardships. When she first arrives at her in-laws' house, she knows nothing about housekeeping, not even how to make coffee. However, over time, she learns everything she needs to know - fetching water, mending clothes, milking cows, etc. To survive, she learns all these tasks. For someone born in the 1980s and as a third-generation Chinese immigrant, the hardships mothers endured are a part of my early memories. Elsa’s first challenge is her relationship with her husband. Getting pregnant was a mutual decision and responsibility, and her husband initially wanted to be a good husband. However, he becomes indifferent, resorting to drinking to escape reality. He later leaves the family, abandoning Elsa and their 2 children, seeking a different life away from his hometown. The second challenge is the misunderstanding from her daughter, who blames Elsa for her father's departure. This forces Elsa to battle life’s struggles while trying to mend her relationship with her daughter. The third challenge is simply surviving. Elsa follows the path her husband took when he left, only to find that working over ten hours a day earns her just 50 dollars - about 5 dollars an hour. This meager amount is insufficient to support herself and her two children. She has to work relentlessly to make ends meet. Despite these challenges, she perseveres. The overall tone of the book is quite oppressive. It feels as though Elsa is perpetually suffocated by her burdens, and her story made me feel very depressed. None of these hardships were what Elsa wanted, but she had no other choice. Beyond its narrative, the book also highlights the plight of interstate migrants in 1930s America. These migrants faced severe discrimination and worked under slave-like conditions. The stark contrast between their living and working conditions and the America of today is shocking. The title, The Four Winds, suggests that no matter which direction the wind blows, one must ultimately face reality. Escape is futile. 3.9 / 5 stars

Lt. Eve Dallas is called to the scene of a murder - a homeless woman's battered body tossed in the dumpster like yesterday's trash. While working the scene, she gets a call to another scene - walls torn down in an old building under renovation reveals the skeletal remains of a woman and her fetus. Two cases, at least thirty years apart with unknown victims - one homeless and desolate, the other with items that indicate wealth. As always, Eve treats both cases and victims the same. She stands for them both working tirelessly until she identifies and then reaps justice for them equally. Questions arise about the murders close proximity to each other and as Eve digs in, it becomes clear they may share a connection. Forgotten In Death lives up to its name . . . Finally. After a long Droughtlander filled seven years, saved by an awesome Starz series, we have the new Diana Gabaldon “Outlander” novel – “Go Tell the Bees that I am Gone” – in our reading hands. And never have I been more-happy going into the holiday season… Thank you, Diana, thank you. So where do I start with my review of “Go Tell the Bees that I am Gone”, the ninth book in Diana Gabaldon’s bestselling “Outlander” series, which is also a highly-rated television show getting ready to air its sixth season on Starz? How do I put into coherent words the ongoing thoughts and emotions running through my head after finishing this continuing grand opus of historical adventure with a unique twist of science fiction? I think that transparency requires me to simply start with - “My name is Scott and I am an Outlander fan…” Over the last two to three years, I have obsessively devoured all eight books in this unbelievably creative and awesomely well-written series, enjoying each of them immensely. There are so many elements, including history, time travel, mystery, adventure, drama, and yes, there’s romance too. Each book is epic and overwhelms with rich background, complex plotting, authentic characters, and strong dialog. All of those elements blend together in one of the most unique and multi-layered mythologies I have ever experienced. It is one that cannot be compared to any other series in any genre. And each book just continues to build on the previous one in an amazing tapestry of storytelling. Multiple plotlines find ways to surprise and connect in wonderful ways. I can only speak for myself, but I am living proof that men can read and tremendously enjoy the Outlander series. For those who are not already diehard fans, Claire Randall is a 20th century doctor who survived going back through the ancient stone circle back and forth in time. There she met Jamie Fraser, an 18th century Scot who was involved in the Jacobite uprising against England and they were forced to marry. She later returned to the present to bear and raise his child when he was assumed killed in battle. Twenty years later, when their daughter, Briana is grown, Claire discovers he survived and she risks everything to return through the stones to Jamie. Later, Brianne and her husband, Roger, join them in the untamed frontier of North Carolina as they build a new future together as a family while the rebellion against England has grown into a war for independence. When “Go Tell the Bees that I am Gone” begins, the American Revolution is in high gear as the British armies continue to wear down the rebel armies. After being reunited with their daughter, Brianna and her family, Claire and Jamie try to settle down into a peaceful family life on Fraser’s Ridge. However, the war is spreading from the larger cities into the backcountry of the Carolina’s, where loyalists are terrorizing rebel supporters and burning down their homes and destroying their farms. Things are getting worse for Jamie. As a landlord, his tenants are becoming divided in their loyalties between the crown and the colonies, and Jamie is going to need to act fast before he and his family are outnumbered by those who support the British. For Brianna and Roger, returning to the past brings them danger as his new ministerial calling pulls him unexpectedly into the middle of the rebel battle to retake Savannah. Brianna also faces her own personal challenges that include dealing her half-brother, William, and the anger he’s working through following the discovery of his true father and perceived betrayal from Lord John. As the Revolutionary War pulls Claire and Jamie’s family into the front lines of an important battle, they will be forced to face not one, but two enemies from the past. One who is trying to take Fraser’s Ridge away from them, and another one, who has a far deadlier outcome planned for Jamie and those closest to him… Covering the time period of June, 1779 through February, 1781, Gabaldon moves these four inter-connected storylines – Claire and Jamie, John Grey and William Ransom, Brianna and Roger, and Ian and Rachel – forward, building on family history, conflict from the colonies struggling in their war for freedom, and hidden enemies that threaten the peace at Frasier’s Ridge. It’s an expansive, but easy read, moving back and forth (a bit disjointedly) between the various storylines, and clocking in at 969 pages in my Kindle reader. Like previous books, Gabaldon introduces and returns to previous storylines, characters, and plot elements over the first several hundred or so pages, setting up several emotional payoffs layered throughout the book, including moments in the spotlight for each of her primary characters. After finishing this opus and taking time to process it, I noticed various feedback on social media from other hardcore Gabaldon and Outlander fans. It seems that there are more than some that are disappointed in this outing. Some have felt that the book was slow and not a lot happened, compared to previous books in the series. Some have also commented that it was disjointed and jumped around a lot between characters and moments in time. I can see those trains of thought, but only to a degree. My fear is that this may be a reflection of expectations increasing exponentially (and unfairly) during the buildup of the seven year long wait for this ninth book to finally get released and it appears that my thoughts may be more in the minority. First of all, while reading this book, I felt several similarities to book 5 – “The Fiery Cross” – in which several plots and characters were introduced and set-up for later development. The same approach was used in this book as well as a lot of reflection on past events that led the characters to their current moments in time. The first couple of hundred pages or so were spent on getting everyone together and catching up on the current events. The next several hundred pages focused on introducing new characters, bringing back previous characters, and developing plotlines against the backdrop of trying to survive the daily life of frontier living and the ever presence influence of the war. Finally, the last two to three-hundred pages brings those plots together, providing some closure, and some key revelations that serve as a wait-until-the-next-and-last book in the series for resolution. Yes, there were reasons to say it was slow and less eventful than other books. Yes, there were reasons to argue it was a bit disjointed at times. Even with all that less than positive feedback, I enjoyed it. I enjoyed it all. I liked how the daily challenges of living on Frasier’s Ridge paralleled the struggled of the war. There were rushes of wartime action and then moments that slowed down and focused on the family and individual members. I loved the time Brianna spent getting to know William better, the unraveling of Frank’s book in terms of determining Jamie’s outcome, Ian reconciling his family past, Jenny’s unique new relationship, and especially the private intimate moments that Claire and Jamie enjoyed together. I think that having more shorter chapters in this book (155 of them, which I think is the highest amount in any of the books) helped contribute to the feeling of it being disjointed and hopping around between characters more than usual. Still, I have no qualms in saying that Gabaldon has many masterful strengths as a writer, including plotting, character, scenes, and dialog. Her plotting is well-planned, multi-layered, detailed in whatever time period is involved, and full of many twists that lead to future surprises and outcomes. For example, this time Gabaldon brings plot secrets that have been percolating for two or more books previously to a high boil. She grabs your attention and requires every one of your senses as you delve into her world. Her characters are rich, complex, and humanely flawed. Each have their own unique personalities, motivations, and attributes. You cannot stop yourself from loving the good guys and hating the bad guys, but more importantly, each and every character is authentic and three dimensional. You can picture them clearly in your mind with real features and smell the sweat on their brow. What I especially appreciated was how Gabaldon reflects the length of love in a long-term relationship. Claire and Jamie are older and not as strong and nimble as they once were. They have grandchildren and family to take care of and worry about. They have made enemies and are in constant worry about the ravages of war being thrust upon them. Others may not agree, but I find Gabaldon’s ability to make their daily activities in the past interesting and inspiring. To me, there’s magic in the challenges they face, whether it be nature, mankind, or beast. And although there weren’t as many earth-shattering or character-shocking moments in this book, it still kept my full attention without a problem. Overall, “Go Tell the Bess That I am Gone” is another excellent and enjoyable outing for Gabaldon. One that builds on the history and foundation before, and hopefully sets up for a final book that will be memorable. Although this one may not the best in the series, it is not the worst. However, for me, there is no worst book; no book in the series is less than 4-stars out of 5 for me. For me, she has found a way to create unforgettable characters that I have come to know and deeply care about. I am not afraid to admit that I have shared some deeply personal moments with them, including laughter, struggle and challenge, pain and sadness, and tears of joy in the things that matter most – family, sacrifice, honor, and love. I think that down the road after the tenth and expected final book in the series is out, this one will stand the test of time better, and the initial negative feedback that is currently being expressed, will gradually fade away. Now I join the rest of Outlander fandom and wait ever so patiently for the next five years or so until that final book gets published… Until then we’ll rely on the show…

A sprawling family epic in 10th century England! THE EVENING AND THE MORNING is a great story. There’s no doubt about that. But I’d never give it the same breathless 5-star rating that I awarded to PILLARS OF THE EARTH when I unhesitatingly added that novel to my list of lifetime favourites because (in my opinion at least) THE EVENING AND THE MORNING, is derivative self-plagiarism - an edited, rewritten version of PILLARS OF THE EARTH simply relocated in time by two centuries. That doesn’t for even a second mean that I didn’t enjoy it. I just couldn’t shake that “Been there, done that” feeling throughout the entire novel! At the close of the first millennium, England is ostensibly ruled by Ethelred (now known by the unflattering epithet of “Unready”), ruthlessly harassed in the east by marauding Vikings and in the west by brutal bands of Welsh warriors. Dreng’s Ferry, which will evolve into the thriving medieval “metropolis” known in the 13th century as Kingsbridge Priory, was little more than a brief traveler’s resting place in the middle of nowhere – an alehouse; a stable to rest, water, and feed the horses; and a whorehouse in which sex-starved (and less than scrupulously discerning) travelers could avail themselves of the service of underage female slaves. Just as he did in PILLARS OF THE EARTH, Follett uses the history of the era to full advantage and masterfully weaves the fundamental ingredients of 11th century England slowly arising from the bleakness of the Dark Ages into a stirring plot that will keep you reading well into the wee hours - the push and pull of church versus state as bishops tussle with nobility and archbishops squabble with the king and routinely ignore the attempted enforcement of his rulings or fines; the very tenuous and fluid definition of title and property ownership; the nature of military strategy and the frightful concept of in-close hand to hand combat in the middle ages; markets, trade fairs and the nature of commerce and business licences of the day. Follett has populated this novel with an astonishing cast of memorable characters whose personalities, weaknesses, strengths, habits and physical descriptions are portrayed with a remarkable level of detail. Indeed, each of the characters might be said to be a metaphorical stand-in for a human characteristic that is a shoe-in for inclusion in a novel of this type – Edgar (one might call him “Edgar the Good” or “Edgar the Strong”) represents strength, courage, loyalty, perseverance, and unquenchable romantic love; Wynstan and his domineering mother Gytha are the stand-ins for evil and psychopathic narcissism; Aldred, the far-seeing, idealistic monk shows us pride, intelligence, tolerance, wisdom, and self-effacement; Ragna is foresight, brilliant Machiavellian political savvy, and feminism suffering under the yoke of universal misogyny; Edgar’s half-brother Garulf shows masculine strength and a warrior’s ability abused and wasted by greed, a brutish stupidity and complete lack of leadership ability; well, the list goes on and on. The good guys will make you laugh, weep and cheer and the bad guys will make your skin crawl. But - trust me - bad or good, you won't be forgetting these folks any time soon! (And on somewhat of a sidebar, it would seem to me that Wynstan’s conduct as a bishop illustrates reasonably clearly that, as an author, Follett has little constructive or positive to say about organized religion’s place in the history of mankind. Just my opinion, of course!) Follett's story-telling is as ambitious as the setting in which he has chosen to place it. Like other modern extended family tales such as Archer's KANE AND ABEL, John Jakes' THE KENT FAMILY CHRONICLES or the classic Dickens' NICHOLAS NICKLEBY, we are treated to a smorgasbord of emotions and characteristics - love and hate, strength and weakness, devotion and loyalty, dishonour and deceit, intelligence and bone-headed stupidity, altruism and selfishness, stubbornness and obsession, bravery and cowardice. An extraordinary, compelling drama, THE EVENING AND THE MORNING deserves to be on your bookshelf. The evolution of Dreng’s Ferry from that questionable pit-stop at a river-crossing into a proud bishopric sets the table for its ultimate conversion to an archbishopric and the site of Tom Builder’s magnificent cathedral in PILLARS OF THE EARTH. Paul Weiss

I have a lot of thoughts about this, the first being: for goodness sake, get an editor in here. Nothing needs to be this long. The second thought being: damn it, though, this was pretty good. I didn't know until I was well into the story that Alchemised is a reworking of a very popular Dramione fanfic (Manacled) and I don't particularly care. It didn't read anything like Harry Potter and, aside from hair descriptions, Helena and Ferron don't remind me of Hermione or Draco in any way. No, Alchemised is a necromancer fantasy with excellent world-building and characters made deeply complex by the realities of war. It is primarily a love story, of sorts, but I understand why the publishers have tried to distance it from the romantasy genre. It feels tonally very different from a lot of mainstream romantasy, definitely much darker than any of the stuff I’ve read or sampled, with depictions of rape, graphic torture, trauma, suicidal ideation, eugenics and cannibalism. That being said, there can be no doubt that the book centres the main relationship. There is a plot outside of it about war and alchemy and necromancy, and there are compelling twists and turns, but the main conflict of the novel still feels firmly between Helena and Ferron. Genre quibbles aside, by far my favourite aspect of the book is the clever use of a nonlinear narrative. We begin in the present of the story where Helena awakes to discover the Eternal Flame have lost the war and she is now a prisoner of the Undying. But, worse still, she is missing years of memories. As the Undying try to dig through her brain and uncover what she is hiding, she herself wonders why someone would have hidden part of her mind. What were they so desperate to hide? I've seldom known a part 2 so drastically change my view of part 1. The discovery of Helena's hidden memories makes some things make more sense, while completely shocking on others. I thought this framing was nothing short of brilliant. It made me want to go back and read part 1 again with my new insight. But let's get to the romance, because it will make or break it for readers. I'd recommend this for those who enjoy darker romances, because the truth is that the relationship is messed up, heartbreaking and, for a long time, unhealthy. I myself am wary of trauma romance, but I think this is one of few cases where the context makes it understandable. Both Helena and Ferron are victims of war, and I think the author depicts how deep the trauma of war penetrates. Not just for the obvious victims enslaved on the losing side, but also for those carrying out horrific orders out of fear. A note on rape in this book— (view spoiler) Read this if you want to read a dark tale about war, necromancers and fucked up people. Do not read this if you're looking for a healthy depiction of romance. In the end, this is a story about two irrevocably damaged people who've seen and committed atrocities. I won't sit here and try to convince you that either one is good or just misunderstood. They are what they are. And war made them that way.

Yikes, that was pretty full on. Mercy is the 4th book in the Atlee Pine series by David Baldacci. The whole series is pretty much about Pine looking for her twin sister, Mercy, who was abducted about 30 years ago when they were both 6 years old. Atlee herself was left for dead and had a serious head injury. Now Pine and her redoubtable admin assistant, the 60 something Carol Blum, are on a sabbatical from the FBI and are following every little clue to find Mercy In this book Pine has come closer than ever before to finding her sister and she learns who her biological father is. The first part of the book focuses, for the first time, on Mercy herself. We learn how she escaped captivity, how abused she was, how she struggled in the early years of her ‘freedom’ with further abuse and addictions and how, finally, she has made a life for herself, albeit not an easy one. She is very tall and phenomenally strong and earns some of her income by cage fighting in which she is a formidable opponent. Pine has managed to track down Desiree Atkins, the wife in the couple with whom Mercy was forced to live for many years and who was her main abuser. Another step closer and the two sisters are getting closer to actually meeting. Mercy is now calling herself El (Eloise) Cain. One day she makes a serious mistake. She beats up a man who was beating up his girlfriend. After he pulled a knife and then a gun on her she has no qualms about thrashing him in self defence but she did make sure to leave him alive. Unfortunately the man later died in hospital and his brother is a very wealthy and influential man - now seriously bent on revenge. The rest of the story is about how that plays out. I was almost too scared to read on at this point as I thought it would be brutal. And I was not wrong. Baldacci certainly knows how to write suspense and action scenes. There was a lot of fighting but when I saw what the man chasing Mercy was planning for his revenge, I quailed. Yep I’m a scaredy-cat! But I also had to find out how it would end. Of course! Baldacci’s characters are often either good guys or bad guys but Mercy was, certainly because of the harsh life she’d lived, very much in the grey zone. Carol Blum is a delight as she is almost motherly but also very smart, intuitive and efficient. People underestimate her at their peril. This was very much an action book and it was fast paced throughout. If you want to catch your breath you have to stop reading. Without giving away the ending I DO think this will be the last book in the series, although I would be happy to read more about Pine and her wonderful ‘minder’, Blum. This fast-paced thriller is the culmination of 3 previous books in a search for Atlee Pine’s sister, Mercy. Naturally, any book from a series can be read as a stand-alone but I would seriously advise against attempting to read this without reading at least one of the previous books. Sure, it’ll be entertaining but without the crucial context of what has gone before there will be a great deal that will be missed. Atlee Pine, the FBI agent, along with her trusted assistant Carol Blum has been on the trail of the twin sister who was abducted from their bedroom 30 years earlier and it has taken them on a string of harrowing and dangerous escapades until ultimately plonking us hot on the trail of what appears to be a tearful and satisfying reunion. But, of course, that’s far from how Mercy plays out. In true David Baldacci thriller style, there are a couple of whack-jobs standing in the way of any type of reunion with the lives of both Pine women, not to mention Blum, in grave danger. As we learned way back in the first book of the series, Long Road To Mercy, Atlee Pine’s sister was kidnapped and Atlee was given a fractured skull as the remaining twin. We then found out that Mercy was being held in deplorable conditions and was subjected to the most horrifying of torture and degradation. So the question on our minds (as well as Atlee’s mind) is whether Mercy has come out of it totally mentally scarred. This is only one of the questions that are answered in this resolutionary volume. Rather than simply find her sister and enjoy a tearful reunion, things get rather complicated thanks to an earlier confrontation in which Mercy played savior to a domestic abuse situation. Her actions have put someone on her tail who has the means and motivation to seek his own kind of retribution. Rather predictably, just as contact between the sisters is to be made, the fly in the ointment makes himself known and chaos ensues. While I’m satisfied that there was always going to be an edge of the seat confrontation taking place in what has been a thrilling series so far, I wasn’t particularly happy with the motives of the bad guy here. Now, I know this is fiction and it’s all made up, but this just felt too made up. He just wasn’t a believable villain…at all. Not only that, I felt his motivations for pursuing Mercy and Atlee were weak and his actions were illogical And this wasn’t helped by one particular fight scene towards the very end of the book which was just too ludicrous for words. The quad-series deserved a stronger ending than this. This last part aside, I have enjoyed this series a great deal and was very satisfied with the full explanation that is provided after the dust has settled. We’re provided with a suitable outcome that serves to form a well-composed 30 year long tragic mystery.

This is the fourth and final book in the series in which FBI agent Atlee Pine has been searching for her long ago abducted twin sister through the last 3 novels. And her sister happens to be named Mercy. Which means...we (us readers) can finally have closure with the long-awaited ending to this long ago crime. Yes, we have been waiting this long. What I can say is that Atlee has found proof that Mercy escaped those who captured and imprisoned her many years earlier. Just knowing that she escaped, though, is more than enough incentive for Atlee and Carol to take a leave from the FBI to concentrate even harder on tracking her down. Needless to say, their journey is fraught with roadblocks, several of which are life-threatening (overdone, IMHO, to the point at which I said, "Whoa, nobody could survive this." But then, I suppose it was a cake walk for Mercy, whose captive years are described in even more horrific detail. Put another way, if explicit barbarian-style torture isn't your cup of tea, you'll want to skip parts of this one. It's also heavier on melodrama than usual, which was a bit of a turn-off for me as well. Overall, though, while I won't say this, the fourth book in the series, is my favorite, it was entertaining as always. It certainly brought the series to full circle - wrapping up several loose ends and leaving me with only the question of what happens next. So hey, I've followed the series from the beginning, so if there are other chapters to follow, count me in!

It’s that time of year – Fall – when one of my favorite mystery/suspense writers - David Baldacci - publishes a new book. This time we get the fourth novel in his Atlee Pine series, a female FBI agent with a gigantic chip on her shoulder. Agent Pine is 35 years old, at least five feet eleven inches tall, and in fantastic physical shape (as most of Baldacci lead characters are). She’s competed in MMA fighting and kickboxing, and is a serious weightlifter. Serious enough to have barely missed qualifying for the 20014 Athens Olympics. But Pine also has a dark past. She had a twin sister, Mercy, who is no longer around. When the two were both six years old a stranger snuck in their bedroom window, played eeny, meeny, miny, moe with them, and snatched her sister away, never to be seen or heard from again. Atlee was left behind, traumatized for life. This fourth book – “Mercy” – is crucial, because Pine has spent the previous three investigating what happened to her twin sister, and this one is supposed to be the payoff in that search (yes, seriously three books to get us here…). “Mercy” starts out with where the previous book ended, with the startling discovery of why her parents abandoned her and went into hiding, and how her sister, Mercy, was abducted and lived as a prisoner. What was even more important is that it appears Mercy was able to escape from her kidnappers and got away from them. Could that possibly mean Mercy could still be alive? And if so, can Atlee track her down? Because most of what happens in this payoff book, I will stay away from sharing the plotlines so as not to ruin any key plot points or give away any spoiler moments. What I will say is that this would be a hard book to read if you haven’t read the first three books in this series. Without having invested time into reading the prior books, you will not only lack the necessary understanding of what happened up to this point, you will not experience the full richness of the emotional payoff that has built up over the four-book set. In essence, this is really one big story told over four continuous books. This one takes a while to get going as Atlee Pine and her assistant/mentor Carol Blum, pick up from where they left off in their search for Atlee’s twin sister Mercy, whom they hope is still alive and can be found. However, once it gets moving, Baldacci picks up the pace and turns up the temperature to steady boil throughout the last three hundred of four hundred pages. Once the multiple and inter-connected storylines get rolling, there’s no looking back. Only full steam ahead with the pedal to metal in classic Baldacci thriller style. What I can say (without ruining anything) is that I thoroughly enjoyed the roller coaster ride that was the last three hundred pages. It was fast-paced, full of twists and turns, and a thrill ride of a read. More importantly, the most important question to answer is this – was Baldacci able to deliver on the ending that has been building over four books? Was the pay-off worthy of the reading investment? For me, the answer was an easy Yes! It’s hard not to provide any reasons or support without giving anything away, but I will try. We, as readers, have certain expectations when it comes to payoffs. And purposely choosing to deliver a mystery storyline over four books is not easy. Only giving away so many clues while keeping the tension and storylines moving over multiple books is even harder to accomplish. Not just any writer can pull it off. I am rather surprised and pleasantly pleased that Baldacci was able to map out such a mystery over those books, while keeping my interest through the whole thing. I admit to some moments of frustration, but they were few for the most part. However, I also agree with many other readers, that this storyline could not be dragged out more than four books. It needed to come to an end and it a good end it was. In this concluding book, “Mercy”, Baldacci brings Atlee Pine’s search for her missing twin, Mercy to a strong and rewarding conclusion, delivering a layered and action-packed adventure that brings the multi-book story arc to a grand climax that will leave most readers with a well-delivered resolution. As to whether there will be more Atlee Pine adventures in the future, I openly throw my vote in for more, especially to see how things can be further developed based on the outcomes of this book. But if her adventures are to end with “Mercy”, then I can still honestly say this is a fitting end honorable way for Atlee Pine to go out…

One of the first things you'll be told as a budding writer is to 'show' not 'tell'. Because apparently audiences (ie. readers) find it boring (or at least less engaging) and feel patronised. At least that's why I've always assumed you don't provide laborious detail in your prose. David Baldacci very much breaks that rule in the beginning of his latest novel, Mercy, providing backstory on FBI Agent Atlee Pine and her sister, kidnapped three decades earlier. And I for one appreciated it because, even though I've read the entire series AND re-read my review of Mercy's predecessor, Daylight , I was a bit murky on the details. So Baldacci's summary - succinct yet informative - hit the spot. So... not-so-spoiler-alert... Mercy Pine is alive. Atlee may not know if she remains so 19 years after her escape from the Atkins', but we know because we're quickly introduced to Eloise Cain who we learn 'was' Rebecca Atkins... who happened to escape her abusive adoptive parents. I appreciated that Baldacci didn't waste a lot of time keeping us guessing IF Eloise (El) is Rebecca. But of course the twist is that El has no idea she was once Mercy Pine. So when the FBI puts a call-out to locate her she assumes it was because of what happened when she escaped the Atkins'. Of course (although she doesn't know it) El's not in trouble and there's no mystery or issue in the present, given her kidnappers are no longer a threat. Or at least there wouldn't be if El hadn't inadvertently pissed-off a wealthy businessman (and cold-hearted thug) by intervening when his drunk ex-con brother violently attacked his girlfriend. El puts the event behind her so has no idea she's incurred the wrath of a man who puts a hired killer - Britt Spector, a former FBI agent - on her tail. I was supposed to only read part of this book when I opened it, but as is often the case with Baldacci's action-packed and well-paced thrillers, I kept going until I was finished. It becomes a race against time with Atlee and Carol trying to track down Mercy, unaware someone else is after her. Baldacci didn't belabour our introduction to Mercy here and he doesn't overplay the eventual meeting of the sisters (and what comes after). I think it takes some skill and experience at one's craft to not be tempted to over-dramatise something you've spent books building up to. I've really enjoyed this series and realise it may potentially end with this book. However... through the introduction of Spector, Baldacci has potentially given us a brand new protagonist and / or series which may see Atlee and / or Mercy pop up again. Wilde was living wild in the woods (get it?) thirty years ago. No one, including him, knew his name, his exact age, where he came from, his parents’ names, were or how long he had been surviving alone in the woods. He has vague memories, foggy nightmares, but even as an adult all he remembers is scavenging to survive and playing with his friend, Adam. He's an adult now, but still more comfortable being on his own, living in the woods and keeping even those who love him at arm’s length. Raised in foster care, he excelled in school and even more so in the military where he was a member of an elite group taking part in secret missions. When his godson asks him to locate a missing girl, Naomi Pine, he knows there is more to the story than his godson, Matthew is telling him. Soon Wilde begins his investigation and enlists Matthew's Grandmother, TV personality and lawyer, Hester Crimstein, who in my opinion steals the show. She is a tough old broad that is also va-va-voom! She seriously is the best, and I am purposely not saying more about her. Soon, it becomes clear (as it always does in this genre) that there is more going on with the various characters in this book than meets the eye. Soon, Wilde will be up against those with secrets, those with hired muscle, those who will do anything to uncover those secrets and those who will do anything to keep those secrets hidden. Coben does not disappoint in this book, what begins as a missing person investigation quickly turns into so much more. This book touches on politics, power, romance, bullying, quilt, family, loss, the impact of secrets and how social status can either help or hurt a person. There are a lot of characters in this book and Coben gives them unique personalities and voices. The plot moves at a fast pace as Wilde and others attempt to figure out just what the heck is going on and why. This is another solid book by Coben. He delivers time and time again and this book is no exception! I found myself engrossed in the book, completely glued to the pages, waiting for the reveal and completely enjoying the book from the very first to the very last page. There are so many characters in the book that I just want to see/read again. Articulate! (and yes, at some point in the near future I am going to answer my phone this way!) Well written, well thought out, perfectly paced, captivating and entertaining. Highly recommend! 3.5. The Boy from the Woods sees Hester Crimstein returning to Westville, New Jersey, the township where she raised her family. Fans of Harlan Coben's work will likely be familiar with the character, who has featured in (I count six) of his previous books as a shrewd, sarcastic, tough but fair Criminal Litigator. And she's still all those things in this one, but the plot delves into Hester's personal life, and past, and we are shown a softer more vulnerable side to her. Now seventy, Hester is widowed, and there's even a romance on the horizon, a subplot that was just delightful. Hester was most definitely the highlight – her witty retorts and comebacks had me in stitches. Hester’s teenage grandson Matthew approaches her on the set of her television show – Crimstein on Crime – to ask for her help. A classmate of his, Naomi Pine, has been absent from school for a week, and Matthew is worried about her, but is cagey about why. It soon comes to light that Naomi has been the victim of severe long-term bullying and hazing by the popular kids. Has she run away, or has something more sinister befallen her? Hester enlists the expertise of Wilde, her son's best friend growing up. Known as The Boy From the Woods, Wilde has no past prior to being found living in the State Forest near Westerville over thirty years ago – estimated age at the time six to eight. Just as Hester and Wilde are getting closer to the truth of Naomi's disappearance another student goes missing. With the exception of Hester, I have to say that Coben's latest installment wasn't my favourite. Too political rather than domestic for my tastes, and pissing contests, and punch-ups, between security firms don't really float my boat. Wilde was enjoyable, and the author's exceptional use of his dialogue helped me like him, but the character is a complete cliché - you'll see what I mean. Twists wise, there were some unexpected surprises, but the plot wasn't as complicated and compelling as normal. Since the author's known for his recurring characters, I'm guessing Wilde will return at some point? I'm happy to read more about him, but here's hoping the crime is more interesting. Some plot elements from Run Away (his novel from last year that I preferred over this one) made a cameo appearance, but didn't spoil anything, so it's safe to read this one beforehand, if you like the sound of this one better. I read this over a day and couldn't put it down, so even though it's not his best effort, The Boy from the Woods still held my attention. Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called “Ready Player Two.” And get through it I did, with pleasure. This is a book where I think in order to heed a review, you need to know the reviewer. So here are some quick deets on me: I grew up in the glorious ‘80s. We were home alone a lot. When it rained it was purple. I ate at a breakfast club so many times I knew the menu by heart. I LITERALLY HAD A CAT NAMED FERRIS. If any of the above brings a nostalgic smile to your face, there’s a good chance you’ll get a great big kick out of "Ready Player Two." Because I could easily play along in figuring out a few of the riddles the characters unraveled, I enjoyed this book so much. I also got a sense that Ernest Cline enjoyed writing it. If he got a lot of cash for the effort, or if he didn’t plan on writing a sequel when he wrote "Ready Player One," makes absolutely no difference to me. Am I even giving it a fair chance going in since my expectations are already set so high? Yes, all of these things went through my mind as I started Ready Player Two. But there was no way I wasn’t going to read it! I mean, you really have to be ready to nerd out over very specific pop culture topics for several hours. So, only click if you have finished the book or if you don’t care about spoilers: (view spoiler) Should you read this? If you liked Ready Player One like I did, you may like this. But, be aware that I am seeing many Ready Player One fans give it one or two stars. So, proceed with caution and expect anything! Are you ready to nerd out for several hours? And, I mean REALLY nerd out! Like – go overboard into a raging sea of nerdiness? Open a can of pure, concentrated nerd-juice and chug it until you have to rush to the restroom and purge yourself of all the pop-culture?? And then, after all that, eat a big, fat nerd sandwich? If you cannot answer yes to all of this or are not sure you are at least okay with this being the experience, then you need not read this book . . . if you do and didn’t listen me, don’t come back and say that I didn’t warn you!
