"David and Cheryl Burroughs are living the dream - married, a beautiful house in the suburbs, a three year old son named Matthew - when tragedy strikes one night in the worst possible way." This mystery kept me on the edge of my seat to find out what happened next. It is propulsive, twisty, and kept me guessing.

Harlan Coben has once again come up with a plot that is as unique as it is compelling with his stand alone thriller I Will Find You. Right from the first page there are questions just begging to be answered just by meeting David Burroughs who’s locked up in prison, convicted of killing his baby son. He has always protested his innocence but has become resigned to his fate, taking beatings and accepting his now failed marriage and loss of all friends. It’s not until his sister-in-law Rachel visits him to show him a photo that may, just may, show a boy in the background that could be his son that his life kickstarts again. It’s from this flicker of a possibility that the touchpaper is lit and the action takes off in the most unbelievable fashion. Not only does David have to get himself out of prison but he also has to confirm that the boy is his son. Finding answers to the many, many questions that are racing through his mind is made difficult by the fact that he has to evade the police who are closing in on him. From one little clue in the background of a photo, David manages to take his quest from Maine to New York and through to the wilds of the retirement capital, Florida. If all thrillers were delivered with this type of frenetic action from page 1 I’d be a happy boy. Sure, his method of escape is a little convenient at the top and the close calls are predictable through the middle stages, but that’s forgiven by the sheer entertainment value. A highlight of the book for me was the introduction of a pair of FBI agents who have been tasked with the job of finding David and returning him to his prison cell. Max Bernstein and Sarah Jablonski are one hell of a team who manage to perform the most entertaining interviews with persons of interest. They’re formidable in their approach but also, for the reader at least, wildly amusing in the way they bounce off of each other. They’re very Harlan Cobenesque characters and I definitely want to see more of this pair (please). This is a really good seat of the pants thriller that throws caution to the wind in a bid to completely capture my attention. It worked and I was thoroughly entertained by the imaginative plotting and moments of devilish humour that helped carry the more serious undertones.

Would've been 5 stars if Max and Sarah hadn't been so insufferable.

As of right now, I don’t care about the Night Court, The Court of Dreams (snort), Velaries or the Illyrians. They have all let me down and acted in horrendous ways. I’m only interested in the Valkyries from now on. SJM has gone mad if she believes there’s a pass for all this bullshit. I’m actually mad as hell that I can see the influence of JR Ward all over her writing style because it’s obviously suffering from it. But there’s a reason why I gave this book a high rating and here is why: Nesta Archeron, aka Queen of Queens, was everything I had hoped for and more. Being in her head felt so liberating after so many books in Feyre’s. Suddenly characters were acting “different”, being more honest and thus more horrendous, there were cursing and not that annoying “vulgar gesture” nonsense anymore. You can tell how unreliable Feyre was as narrator. And how much more real and human Nesta is than her sister. Nesta’s journey to healing was arduous, the story didn’t take short cuts, we were there with her in every step of the way. There were good days, there were bad days. The symbolism of the 10.000 steps paralleling her own personal journey was amazing. Nesta truly earned her happiness with teeth and sweat and tears. It felt very satisfying to see her climb that fucking mountain and conquer her life back. Nesta’s breakdown felt cathartic and liberating. I broke along with her, feeling everything she was finally allowing to get out. I was there with her, marveling at the emotional level this book was taking me to. Even though I hated the trek to that lake, with Cassian so uncharacteristically cold and unfeeling towards a broken and suicidal Nesta. He could’ve told her Feyre wasn’t mad at her, instead he chose to let her believe the worse and fester in her own agony. Cassian is not like that in any other moment of the story. It felt contrived and a weak plotdevice to “force” Nesta to the breaking point. The way the story centers around mental health issues and abuse survivors moved me to tears on several occasions. Learning to be vulnerable enough to open up to others, even though their reaction terrifies you, learning to love yourself, even the darkest parts, and accepting your past mistakes and forgiving yourself were the pillars in Nesta’s journey. Nesta is just the most relatable character out there. From reading romance books, her new female friendships, the way she fantasized about two hot men and how she expressed her sexuality. The way she hated and doubted herself at every step. We have all been there. I felt like I was Nesta while reading. Just in this book, Nesta retrieved several millennia-lost magical objects, used them without losing herself, created new magical objects with her bare hands, killed the worst thing trapped in the prison, became a Valkyrie, killed the cursed queen, found her chosen family, helped other women with their trauma and circumstances, mastered 10.000 steps and climbed an impossible mountain, winning the Blood Rite, seduced a man with three dances to the point of receiving a marriage proposal right there, saved the life of her sister, brother-in-law and newborn nephew, sacrificing most of her powers in the process, found her mate and even created a connection with The Mother. Let that sink in. The nivel of baddassery that Nesta Archeron achieved in this book is unfathomable. I loved how a big part of this book was dedicated to the sorority among women and the way most men disrespected and disregarded them. And how, together, they found the way to grow strong and fight back. My Valkyrie babies will always have a special place in my heart. Give me a whole mammoth of a book about the new Valkyries training and fighting in sisterhood. I want to read about Nesta, Gwyn and Emerie training new female recruits and creating an unit ready to fight against any Big Bad coming their way. My Vakyrie sisters fighting together and winning the Blood Rite gave me an overdose of serotonins. Nesta thinking she had found her chosen family in Emerie and Gwyn made me cry. I’m so happy she found people who loved her unconditionally. That little something with Emerie and Mor made me scream. I want them to have their own book. I want Mor to set things right with everyone and be honest and loving with her wife (mate???). I’m imagining Emerie in the middle of the Inner Circle dynamics and I’m loving that. Gwyn felt so special to me from the start. I loved her story, her personality. And more specially, I love the idea of her being Azriel’s mate. I want her to go out there, have a life, and be happy. Imagine her giving some attitude to everyone else in the IC. These people need her, lbr. Nesta and the House were my favorite thing. it was absolutely delightful and brought a smile on my face. And knowing Nesta created the sentienness of the House out of pure loneliness and need for a friend only made me love them even more. I was so afraid something was going to happen to that house, I was ready to die for them!! I know people love to bash SJM for her sex scenes. But as someone who’s read a lot of smut, I have to admit I consider the sex scenes in this book to be some of the best out there. In terms of realness, even with all the over the top nonsense (such as ginormous penises), their desires and the way they acted felt really genuine. The fact that Nesta participated actively, and openly enjoyed sex was a breath of fresh air compared to all these protagonists who lay back and let the man do all the work. Did anyone else notice how women in romance novels don’t give head or pleasure the man in any way but allowing penetrative sex? It’s tedious, unrealistic and boring. Nesta Archeron was created to break all the contrived ideas about what a female character should be like and I’m here for all of it. Cassian is my new favorite male protagonist in the ACOTAR universe. Not only was he funny and sensible, he actively fought for equality among the Illyrians. He was not afraid to show vulnerability and emotions. He openly cried. Like Nesta said, he’s a good man. He was there for Nesta in all the different ways she needed. He fiercely protected and loved everyone in his life. I feel like apart from Nesta, he’s the character who shined the most. The fact that he secretly took dancing lessons for Nesta made me swoon for real. And I love the idea of a big mating ceremony, so everyone knows they love each other 🥺 Overall, I loved Nesta’s journey. The rest was just noise. Fuck them all. Talking about the plot, I think that's the main reason I did not enjoy this book as much as I thought I would. Even though I loved to get to know Nesta, and I adored every Cassian moment, I feel that the plot was really relayed to the background. There were some meetings with Eris and some political moves, but not much happened regarding the threat of war and the quest for allies until the end. I would have liked for the political part of the story to take more room in the book. I was expecting this book to be the beginning of a new trilogy, but it is more of a standalone romance set 14 months after the end of ACOWAR. There are clues that indicate that a bigger plot is coming with the introduction of a new powerful player and new powerful relics, but that's about it. Honestly, there are no major twists in this story, which is surprising. It is a good sexy and funny romance (with steamy hot scenes), and a great story of redemption, acceptance, empowerment, and forgiveness. It's just that in comparison with her other books, this one is quite basic and was missing some intricate details and plot twists that we are used to with SJM (I know that this book is supposed to be more about the characters, but I was still hoping for a better and more complex plot). In C.J. Box’s 25th and newest Joe Pickett novel - “Battle Mountain” – we pick up the pieces of destruction that took place in last year’s book “Three-Inch Teeth”. Rulon’s got his nephew, Mark Eisele, a job working with an elk-hunting guide near Battle Mountain. The problem is that his nephew and the guide have gone missing. Box’s Joe Pickett novels (and related short story collection). Most of them binged over the last six months. And what a rewarding this reading experience has been for me. C.J., Box has done so many wonderful things with these Joe Pickett novels. The plotting, characters, and settings mix together in a masterful recipe in the mystery/thriller genre using a modern western style that delivers a winning formula. In my opinion, his plotting skills are excellent, especially as weaves storylines over multiple books, setting things up in one that will come back and pay off in later books. Box’s strongest skill is his characters, built on the foundation of Joe Picket, his wife, Marybeth, and three daughters, and Joe’s brother from another mother, Nate, who serves as Joe’s physical protector much like Hawk does for Spenser in Robert B. Parker’s classic mystery series. Nate takes care of the things that Joe’s personal code won’t allow him to do. Nate and Hawk are two of my all-time favorite literary characters. I also want to add that C.J. Box writes some of the strongest female characters. Marybeth is smart, analytical, mentally and emotionally strong. So are her daughters – Sheridan, April, and Lucy – each in their own ways. I am strongly endeared to Sheridan, watching her grow into an independent, headstrong woman and falconer. I also look forward to seeing Lucy’s future, which should be bright and full of potential success. It is C.J. Box’s secret sauce that compels his readers to keep coming back over and over again to find out what happens next to them. Joe’s family is our family. Nate’s battles are our battles. Joe and Marybeth’s daughters are our daughters. What happens to them, happens to us. It is personal. And that is the magic C.J. Box delivers to us. It’s why I keep coming back. It is hard to believe that EDGE OF HONOR marks the 24th novel from author Brad Thor to feature American hero and patriot, Scot Harvath. For me, it feels like just yesterday that I was blown away by the first novel, THE LIONS OF LUCERNE --- still my favorite Thor title. Scot Harvath is a newlywed and he and his wife Solvi have just finished six months of globe-trotting purely for pleasure before returning to life in high-stakes spy service for their respective countries of the U.S.A. and Norway. During their lengthy honeymoon there is a new political regime running the U.S. in the form of a new President who has promised to clean up the political landscape and thus far has only heightened the level of criticism from his opponents and those that did not vote for him. Couple that with a series of deadly explosions outside the Vice-Presidential residence that Scot and Solvi were in the middle of, and you quickly realize that something big is in play. One of the decisions made by the new regime was to cut the secret service protection provided to members of the prior Presidential team. This has some of them on the run to the point where some dangerous and well-armed trained killers are hunting them down even invading the location where the Ambassador to Norway resides in Washington D.C. Solvi is called into action to help protect her home countries representatives while Scot is nabbed by the Carlton Group, his employers, to locate and find whoever is behind the very precise and personal attacks being made against current and former political figures in this country. Harvath builds a formidable team of trusted allies around him but is shrewd enough to see that there is a high-stakes conspiracy reaching the highest level of government that he may be working at counterpoint to. His loyalty is to his country and leaders, those who threaten it and are not used to being able to tell who the good guys are. Internal hate groups including many members of national White Supremist groups may be involved along with those who are obviously special forces trained and making up the bulk of the threat to the peace that Harvath must correct. There are not many authors in this genre who truly have their pulse on the machinations of the global political landscape like Brad Thor does. With both domestic terrorism, external threats from long-standing enemies like Russia, and a growing faction of online terrorism, Scot Harvath definitely has his hands full in a situation that is far more complex than he expected while still being firmly planted in the current world we all live in. Brad Thor's latest installment in the Scot Harvath series is another adrenaline-fueled ride that, while not my absolute favorite, is a highly enjoyable and worthwhile read for fans. I found myself tearing through the pages, a testament to Thor's knack for crafting a compulsively readable narrative. What truly stands out in this book is the masterful way Thor weaves in current-day issues. The plot feels eerily ripped from the headlines, creating a sense of urgency and relevance that has never been more effectively executed in the series. It's a powerful reminder of why we turn to thrillers—they often reflect the anxieties and complexities of our real world. The character dynamics were a high point for me as well. The new FBI duo was a fantastic addition, bringing a fresh energy and a compelling subplot to the mix. Their chemistry and contributions were a welcome change of pace and a highlight of the story. On the other hand, the book does fall into a familiar pattern. While I understand this is the core appeal of the genre—the reliable formula we've come to love from authors like Thor and Vince Flynn—it's also worth noting that the unbelievable, almost superhero-like feats of characters such as Scot Harvath are a bright-light reminder that this is fiction and pure escapism. I did feel that the main antagonist was a bit underdeveloped. The villain was, for lack of a better term, "meh," and didn't feel as menacing or memorable as some of Harvath's past adversaries. Despite this minor criticism, the book is a great addition to the series. It's a quick, entertaining read that will satisfy long-time readers and get them excited for what's next.

In Edge of Honor, Brad Thor plunges readers into a covert operation that’s as morally fraught as it is pulse-pounding. The protagonist—a seasoned Navy SEAL—is tasked with a mission that tests not only his tactical skill but his ability to navigate shifting allegiances and political landmines. Thor wastes no time: the action kicks off early and rarely lets up, with tight chapters that propel the story forward like a well-planned assault. What makes this novel stand out is its focus on the mission itself. The stakes are immediate, the objectives clear, and the obstacles formidable. Whether it’s infiltrating hostile territory or decoding the intentions of supposed allies, the tension is constant and grounded in real-world plausibility. Thor’s attention to operational detail adds authenticity without bogging down the pace. While there are echoes of past regrets, they serve more as fuel than distraction. The heart of the book lies in the choices made under pressure—what honor demands when the rules blur and the cost of failure is measured in lives. A must-read for fans of military thrillers who crave action with consequence. Thor proves once again that he knows how to write missions that matter.

"Edge of Honor" by Brad Thor plunges readers into a high-stakes world of political intrigue and global conspiracy, with America's top spy, Scot Harvath, at its center. After a six-month honeymoon abroad with his new wife, Sølvi, Harvath returns to a vastly changed political landscape in the U.S., marked by a new administration and escalating power struggles. His quiet return is shattered by a brazen terrorist attack in Washington D.C. that he and Sølvi narrowly escape, quickly pulling them back into the shadowy world they had momentarily left behind. As the initial attacks escalate and domestic and international threats intertwine, Harvath finds himself navigating a complex web of deceit where trust is fleeting and the very fate of the nation hangs in the balance. The narrative unravels a deep-seated conspiracy involving shadowy elites and potentially even elements within the U.S. government, aiming to bring the country to its knees. With enemies at every turn, including long-standing adversaries like Russia, internal hate groups, and highly trained operatives, Harvath is forced to rely on his unique skills and a newly formed, trusted team to uncover the truth.

** spoiler alert ** In the 24th Scot Harvath thriller, Scot Harvath returns from a six-month honeymoon with his Norwegian wife, Sølvi, to a divided America under a new administration. Planning a quiet Fourth of July, they're thrust into action when gunmen attack protesters outside the vice president's residence, leading to a deadly shootout at the Norwegian Embassy. Harvath, retired from the Carlton Group, protects a former ambassador amid rising unrest over the president's unfulfilled promises. Sølvi guards the Norwegian PM during a NATO summit. Parallel investigations reveal terrorist attacks orchestrated by a cabal of white supremacists, rogue ex-federal agents (FBI, CIA, Secret Service), and Russian intelligence aiming to destabilize the U.S. through disinformation and violence. Harvath teams with the Carlton Group, ex-CIA Chief and FBI agents to uncover betrayals by U.S. officials who want to see the President resign. Harvath saves the day again and he and Solvi enjoy the Independence Day celebration. Another great page turner!

The villains in Edge of Honor live in the shadows... no name, no face, no soul. They don't have the benefit of shouting their plan from the rooftops. (No first name given). Stilwell is a detective with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department who was banished to head the department’s substation at Catalina Island after a dust-up with another detective in the department was resolved by moving Stilwell out of the department’s main headquarters. Of course, the inevitable happens and a dead body is discovered attached to an anchor in the department’s jurisdiction and Stilwell begins his investigation. I've been a big fan of this author for quite some time (just for grins, I counted reviews of those I've posted since I started my book blog in 2013, and there are 13 in there). So getting the chance to sample the first in a new series put a smile on my face for days. Now that I've finished reading, the smile is still there and I'm looking forward to the next installment, but I have to say I'll need more time to really warm up to the new guy in town - if for no other reason than I just can't trust anyone who apparently doesn't have a first name (or maybe that's a plot hook reminiscent of Leroy Jethro Gibbs). Actually, Stilwell is on an island - Catalina Island, to be exact. Once a detective for the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, he irritated the powers-that-be there enough that they deported him to the island where all the department misfits go - a place where they figured he couldn't get in much trouble (and if he did, it wouldn't be their problem). To kick things off, he responds to a report of a female body that's been found at the bottom of the harbor; she's in pretty bad shape and is devoid of any identification except for the purple streak in her hair. At the same time, a buffalo turns up in even worse shape at a local preserve - the victim, presumably, of a poacher. Immediately, Stilwell takes charge of both investigations (with a bit more emphasis on the human victim, understandably). And in short order, he runs afoul of some of his former LA colleagues who now would like nothing better than to kick him to the curb. If that weren't enough, the investigation leads right through the doors of an exclusive men's club on the island - and wealthy, snooty males don't take kindly to having their domain invaded by common folks like the police. The rest of the book is focused on the two investigations, both of which have the potential to end Stilwell's career (if not his life) as well as fleshing out his character and that of several key characters I assume will play central roles in future books. The plot held my attention - as have those of every other book I've read by this author - so I'll definitely be watching for the next one. Meantime, thanks to the publisher, via NetGalley, for the opportunity to get in at the beginning.

Michael Connelley has a stable full of classic characters, including retired Detective Harry Bosch; his half-brother and Lincoln lawyer defense attorney Mickey Haller; the intrepid investigative reporter, Jack McEvoy; and more recently, Renee Ballard, in charge of the LAPD’s Open-Unsolved Unit, where Bosch’s police officer daughter, Maddie volunteers when not working her beat. I greatly liked and appreciated all of three of them for their own strengths, flaws, and drives to do what they think is best to serve the betterment of society. Now, Connelly is introducing a new character to his lineup – Los Angeles County Sherriff’s Detective Stillwell, who has been punished for not playing well with other officers, removed from his homicide investigations on the mainland and exiled to Catalina Island, where he serves as the administrative focal for the local police team. When the book begins, Stillwell has been adjusting to a more peaceful lifestyle outside of the craziness and department politics that came with his prior job. His attention is now focused on the drunk and disorderly incidents that come up with mainland guests visiting the island’s casino every weekend, as well as petty thefts, vandalism, and other petty crimes. He’s even exploring the potential benefits of a new personal relationship with one of the island’s own residents. Except for the local mayor and newspaper editor, life is looking better, that is until… … Detective Stillwell gets a report that a body has been found weighed down in the harbor by a local marina worker cleaning the bottom of a boat. It turns out to be a female Jane Doe, with the only identifying trait of a streak of purple dye in her hair. In addition, Stillwell is also working on a couple of other cases, including the poaching of a federally protected animal on a local reserve, a violent attack at a bar on one of his team’s officers, and the theft of a sculpture from the Black Marlin Club, a private escape the rich and powerful. With an inexperienced and young police team to work with, Stilwell has his hands full. When Stillwell’s boss assigns the Jane Doe case to a Homicide team led by the same Detective Ahearn that caused his banishment to Catalina, Stillwell decides to go around the lines of authority and find the killer on his own while working his other cases. However, the harder Stillwell works, the more Ahearn is determined to get him not only in trouble, but kicked off the force. Ahearn appears to be willing to sacrifice solving the case if it can get Stillwell canned. As Stillwell tries to find justice for Nightshade, a name he has given Jane Doe, he finds that her murder involves closely guarded secrets of a darker side of an island that was intended to be an idyllic escape from the realities of life… First of all, I love me some Michael Connelly crime fiction. For me, he is one of the master storytellers and in my top three favorite writers. Period. No discussion to be had. I have never read a book of his that I didn’t enjoy and I don’t think that I have given him anything less than a 4-star (out of 5) review. So be forewarned, that I have a bias for his writing, but I think it is well defended in truth. If you like the mystery genre and/or crime fiction, Connelly should be on your Mount Rushmore. Having said that, there were several things that I really enjoyed about this one-off from his big three leading star characters, and a few things that I struggled a little bit with. Let’s start with what I liked. Connelly’s no nonsense, straight forward storytelling style and sense is totally present. From the first page, you are pulled into the story as a front seat passenger, right along with Detective Stillwell, another law enforcement officer trying to do the right thing, but not adept enough to avoid the pitfalls that bite you in the backside when you go outside the established political structure of how the Los Angeles Police Department works. Connelly is such a masterful and polished writer. He uses his previous newspaper writing experience to intertwine three ongoing investigations and multiple secondary character relationships in a connected, peal the onion plotting and pacing that provides a gripping reading experience. I felt like I was standing next to Stilwell several times trying to tell him what to do and say as he interviewed various characters of interest as well as when dealing with Ahearn (by the way, what a jerk!). The story and mysteries flowed effortlessly from one scene to another, one conversation to the next, and one twist to another until the multiple climaxes paid off. There was no extra verbiage or unnecessary descriptions taking away from the story’s focus. Connelly uses his characters, plotting, and setting to paint a beautiful canvas. In this particular book, he introduces Catalina, a picturesque island off the coast of Southern California, to play a large role in the location, scenery, and atmosphere of the story. Interestingly enough, Catalina is considered a beautiful tourist destination that can only be reached by a ferry, boat, helicopter, or a private plane. In addition, as Connelly describes in the book, cars and trucks are not allowed to be driven on the island. Transportation is either UTV’s, bicycles, or walking. Catalina provides a great setting for crime fiction and Connelly magnifies its use to the highest degree possible. And now for what I struggled a bit with. I enjoyed the characters for the most part, especially Tash who turned out to be my favorite person in the entire book. I really connected with her, emotionally connected with her arc, and would love to learn more about her in a future book. On the other hand, Stilwell felt like a combination of Harry Bosch and Renee Ballard. Like them, Stillwell is committed to be his being a detective and solving his cases come first over everything else. Over family, friends, hobbies, or any other interests. He takes his professional responsibilities seriously and is addicted to the work to the point that he sacrifices of everything and everyone around him, including the very ones he is in close personal relationships with. That is what drove me a bit crazy while reading this book (and I need to be careful to avoid spoilers hers). Stillwell kept pushing Tash aside and ignoring her feelings and needs because his job is his passion and identity. It’s all that he knows. And even after (be careful here on spoilers) being taken off the investigation and going through a serious emotional event with Tash, Stillwell is right back to his work the very next day and putting aside her stress and fears. Seriously? Come one dude… This is not the way to behave in a relationship… Now, let me be clear. I have come to know and understand this type of obsessive behavior that exists not only in Connelly’s world of criminal investigators, but in many other mystery series too. That by itself is okay. However, what drove me crazy (again, be careful about spoilers) is that when you get to the ending of the book, Stillwell’s never really confronted about his selfish behaviors or made to see that he is being an absolute pig to the very person he proclaims to love. Tash never calls him on it, nor makes him face his disrespectful behaviors. And I thought she would have a completely different reaction at the end of the book than she did. She did not seem bothered by it very much, if at all. Maybe it’s coming in a future book, but how she acted at the end of this one left a level of serious frustration with me. One that is still bugging me as I write this review. As I tried to process my concern, I went and paged through many of the reviews for this book on Goodreads, but I didn’t really see anyone addressing this issue, so it seems like I am in the minority when it comes to readers viewing the situation as I did. So maybe, I should let it go and not worry so much about it. And more importantly, did this issue keep me from enjoying the novel. Absolutely not. The mysteries were strong; the characters and conflict were good; the setting and plotting smooth and well delivered. Overall, this book was a joyful and immersive summer read. Character relationships aside, I look forward to another outing with Detective Stillwell, Tash, and the other characters, including Catalina Island. Although I will always prefer Connelly’s focus be on Bosch, Haller, and Ballard (in that order), I am smart enough to recognize that he has created another unique and flawed character in Detective Stillwell that may grow and develop into a future winner. And let me close with this personal thought… You know what you get with Connelly – an excellent crime fiction experience second to none. Period.

Emotional 4.25 stars “Here’s to no murders next year.” The Last Devil to Die is a mystery about a murdered friend connected to a drug deal gone wrong. When one of their friends is murdered, it is up to The Thursday Murder Club to solve the crime--connecting them to the dark underworld of the drug trade and antiques fraud. This is the fourth book in the series, and while it can be read as a standalone, the emotional aspects of the narrative might not resonate if you are not familiar with the characters or the series. I received an ARC of this book from NetGalley and Penguin Group Viking in exchange for an honest review.

The fourth book in the series may be the most emotional one so far. Here, Richard Osman has fully shifted the focus from “who is the murderer” to “what it means to grow old without disappearing.” There is still a mystery, there is still a death, but they feel more like an excuse to spend a little more time with these characters. The plot once again revolves around a death that initially seems straightforward, but gradually breaks apart into more complex and uncomfortable truths. The investigation is not the tightest in the series and at times feels loose, even secondary. Readers looking for an Agatha Christie–style intellectual puzzle may find themselves slightly disappointed. But that no longer seems to be Osman’s goal. The greatest strength of the book lies in its characters. Elizabeth, Joyce, Ron, and Ibrahim feel more human than ever. Elizabeth in particular is faced with something far more frightening than murder: a loss that cannot be investigated, explained, or fixed. For the first time, Osman almost completely removes the humorous armor and allows the pain to remain quiet, awkward, and real. The humor is still present, but more subdued. Joyce once again brings warmth and lightness, yet even her observations carry a more melancholic tone. The book speaks about death not as a sensation, but as a part of life that arrives without warning and without fairness. This makes the novel more mature, but also heavier to read. My main criticism is that the mystery gets lost among the emotional layers. Some plot threads appear and disappear without leaving a strong impression, and the final reveal is less impactful than the internal changes in the characters. But perhaps this is entirely intentional. The crime is not the center. The people are. Unfortunately, the library I belong to does not yet have the fifth book. But that may actually be a good thing, because it is comforting to know that if I ever want to return to this kind of world, there will already be one waiting for me. **Many thanks to NetGalley, Erica Martirano at St. Martin's Press, and Kristin Hannah for an ARC of this book! Now available as of 2.6!!** "A woman is like a tea bag - you never know how strong she is until you put her in hot water." - Eleanor Roosevelt Frances "Frankie" McGrath knows that nursing school is just the beginning for her...but the men in her life don't quite agree. With her brother heading out to Vietnam to follow in the footsteps of the men in McGrath family, his goodbye party is a wake-up call to Frankie...and she feels a pull she just can't ignore. Why aren't any WOMEN featured on her father's "Wall of Heroes?" In the words of the poet Dylan, the times were 'a-changin' and a 'safe' and sheltered life at home in the California sun just doesn't seem like the right fit for Frankie. She feels compelled to put her skills to use overseas, and to be the first McGrath woman to serve her country as part of the medical corps. Despite her family's protests, Frankie ends up enlisting in the Army Nurse Corps and proudly takes her place alongside other brave men and women ready to save lives - no matter the cost. But Frankie's innocence and lack of experience lead to a rude awakening the minute she hits the soil: her two roommates (who will become besties) Barb and Ethel quickly show her the ropes and remind her not to drink the water...and that the prim and pristine nurse outfits that might work in the States have no place here. Her hooch (slang for a 'thatched hut or improvised living space' is not exactly a cabin from summer camp...and Frankie learns that the type of horrors she's going to see on a daily basis....well, they weren't exactly depicted in her nursing school textbooks. Dealing with the constant threat of ending up a casualty, and learning how to perform surgical procedures on the fly, Frankie has her hands full...and throw in a questionable romantic entanglement or two, and it's CERTAINLY more than she bargained for... Eventually, Frankie's tour comes to an end, and she looks forward to the warm embrace of the family she left behind...but nothing could have prepared her for what she finds when she returns to the States. Not only is she not afforded a hero's welcome...she's met with scorn, ridicule, and a family that seems ashamed of her service. The country itself is divided, and because so many believe the war itself to be a mistake, there are protests, anger, and vitriol coursing through the veins of the citizens of the United States. Frankie is even met with statements like "There were no women in Vietnam," leaving her floored, hurt, and terrified about what a return to civilian life will be like for her and her friends. As tensions continue to rise and Frankie fights for her rights as a Vietnam veteran AND a female in a rapidly changing environment, a flood of mental health struggles threaten to disrupt her life...permanently. Can Frankie learn to process her trauma, fight for her rights AND discover what life after the war looks like for her...or will the aftershocks of a senseless war keep her mired in pain and unable to move forward...at all? If there's one thing that's evident in all of Kristin Hannah's historical fiction, it's that she's spent FAR longer than many of her contemporaries burying herself in research about the time period (and oftentimes, the battle) at hand. Her books have a specific feel to them, one that is simply bursting with detail about the sights, sounds, smells, and look of the scenery in play. However, with all of this detail teeming from each page, I've found that at times it feels like Hannah is OVER explaining and almost justifying what time period we are in a bit TOO often, while simultaneously expecting the reader to have the level of familiarity she does with some of the background of the time period. A great example of this: TaB is mentioned as a beverage of choice many times throughout the book...as if to say, "Remember? It's the 1960s!"...but when intricacies of wartime life and vocabulary a reader who may not be familiar with the Vietnam War much at all (such as myself) such as the aforementioned "hooch" are presented with little explanation...it feels like a missed opportunity. I realize Hannah's books are fiction and not a textbook: however. coming into this book with little context about the war itself and what the day-to-day looked like in Vietnam, THAT would have been interesting to learn, rather than to just surmise what I THOUGHT it might be via context clues. There's a second hallmark of Hannah's writing that was certainly present here: she leans into telling stories of strong women battling the patriarchy, and demonstrating that they are as powerful as men, if not more so. Frankie certainly fits the bill at first glance: she's smart, determined, brave, and even a bit headstrong, and as a reader, at the beginning of the book, I was all in with her journey. However, once you get to actually KNOW Frankie...she's a bit of a mess when it comes to decision making, and to be honest, it made it incredibly hard to empathize with her at times. For a woman so determined to forge her own path and be independent, she relies HEAVILY on her friends to bail her out time and time again (which due to the magic of fiction and storytelling, they are consistently able to drop everything at a moment's notice), and despite CONSISTENT clues that men in her life are toxic, Frankie ignores this information and continues to pursue these options. NOT TO MENTION when she ends up with a wonderful man in her life later on, she basically treats him like The Backup Guy and drops him like a bad habit. This sort of disparity in our MC made her more than a bit unlikable, and despite the empathy I felt towards her overall situation, I also felt like she purposefully got in her own way FAR more than was necessary to make the drama in the story work. There's also the small fact that Frankie is the ONLY person we hear from....for the ENTIRE book. All 480 pages of it. With fascinating side characters like Frankie's two pals Barb and Ethel, and even some of the people she meets after returning home from war that seemed...to be blunt, more likable than Frankie, we only see the turn of events from her perspective. This book felt more like it could have been called "The WOMAN," in all honesty. Aside from not hearing from Frankie's pals, another glaring opportunity that was missed was the chance to hear from ANY of the women in VIETNAM in a real way. There are very few interactions between Frankie and these characters...but I don't see why this needed to be the case. As an author who has made it her mission to tell these type of stories, a way to flesh out this book (and still probably cut down on page count!) would have been to include the perspective of some of the women fighting for survival in their own country, at LEAST in the first half of the book. I would have gladly dropped some of the seemingly endless descriptions of bombs, blood, and some of Frankie's mooning over the aforementioned Bad Guy to hear more of THESE stories. Perhaps the final 'hallmark' of a Hannah book in and of itself is tragedy: there WILL be deaths, and plenty of them. This is also a bit of a pain point for me personally when reading her books, because at times it can be easy to telegraph exactly who will meet their demise...and even sometimes WHEN, for the benefit of the plot. I don't mind a couple of these 'predictable' instances, but with Hannah's books, they can have the feel of a thriller that just didn't know when to quit and has a few too MANY twists. Despite these areas for opportunity in this particular novel, Hannah continues to forge ahead with her long-standing mission of exploring the other side of the coin: rather than a male-dominated, patriarchal view of all things war-related, it is the bold and brilliant women who were the backbone of many a turbulent time. She perhaps could not have picked a more complex conflict to explore, and with such divide about what it means to be a true patriot still ringing true today, this quote from MLK perhaps sums up the ramifications of a nation still feeling the aftershocks today: "The war in Vietnam is but a symptom of a far deeper malady within the American spirit." And if there's anyone with the strength to cure ANY malady...who better than a nurse? 👩‍⚕️ 4 stars

As I have described in previous book reviews, it is time for one of my annual late Fall rituals. The leaves are falling (or if you are in Seattle, the rain is falling). College football is in full gear and the winter holidays are starting. It’s time to build a fire in our fireplace, open the new John Grisham novel, “The Exchange”, and escape into the legal world of thriller fiction. Over the last couple of years, Grisham has been changing things up and trying new approaches rather than just relying on his normal underdog-do-gooder fighting the evil and powerful corporate villains. Last year it was a trip back in time to the crime and corruption on the Mississippi coast from the 1940’s to the 19080’s. This year he revisits the past as well as explores a new type of legal thriller. “The Exchange” brings back Mitch and Abby McDeere, the young couple from Grisham’s first breakthrough novel “The Firm” published back in 1991. “The Firm” told Mitch and Abby’s story of joining the Memphis law firm Bendini, Lambert & Locke following Mitch’s graduation from Harvard Law School. However, the firm was set-up by the mafia to launder illegal money and evade taxes. After the two of them discover the awful secret, their lives are at risk as they try to expose the crimes and flee to safety. “The Firm” was mega-bestseller, launching Grisham’s super-successful career as a legal thriller writer, and a hit movie starring Tom Cruise probably helped contribute some too. In the Author’s Note at the end of “The Exchange” Grisham comments that his readers over the years continue to write to him asking “Will we ever see Mitch and Abby again?” The answer is yes, and 32 years later we the follow-up “The Exchange” to find out what happened to our two fictional heroes. Now, there are a few interesting things about “The Exchange” and how the book is being marketed. First, the it takes place 15 years after the first one, in 2005. The second item of note is that the book cover doesn’t really tell you what the sequel is about. It does two things. It lets you know that Mitch and Abby are living in Manhattan, New York, and that Mitch is a partner in the largest law firm in the world (that’s probably not a surprise). It also teases the new storyline with a vague description that Mitch will find himself in the middle of a “sinister plot” with “worldwide implications” and that “this time there’s nowhere to hide”. When I read the book jacket, I really glossed over that and didn’t really realize that the plot specifics were being held back. When I started reading the book, and things got going, I started to understand that cover description was holding back on purpose. I truly was better off not knowing more about the storylines beforehand. And I am going to do the same, and stay away from sharing the overall plotline so that you can have the same sense of discovery and enjoyment in your reading experience. What an excellent marketing approach – focus on the return of Mitch and Abby without giving anything away about what the new story is about. We, as readers, are so excited to have them return, that this could have almost been a cookbook and we still would have bought it. Sorry, that’s also an inside joke you’ll understand after reading it. It also allows (and here I tread lightly) Grisham to continue his exploration of new areas of the law to explore. Without giving too much away, Grisham expands his scope of the law into international geo-political spectrums. This is what I would refer to as an international political/legal thriller. It is a new and interesting flavor for his readers that it worth taking. Throughout he still sprinkles in his personal views on capital punishment, solitary confinement, and the value of someone’s life in ways that you know are personal and dear to him. Trust me, you are never bored with a Grisham novel, and that is true with this one. The key to Grisham’s success as a writer, shines through in this book. He is a master storyteller and his writing style just demands your attention is such a fluid and effortless manner. His descriptions are brief, focused, and vivid. His dialogs are sharp and flow like a Robert B. Parker Spenser novel at its best. More importantly. Like Stephen King, Grisham is a pure in heart storyteller, and his storytelling skills are pretty flawless – smooth and flowing prose with no wasted or unnecessary words, a constant focus on moving the conflict forward while pulling on your emotional heart strings. I especially appreciated that Abby’s role was expanded and she played an essential part in the storylines. She and Mitch were equal partners and her role was just as important as his. I also like the continued use of the Scully & Pershing law firm by Grisham. It’s Mitch’s firm in this book, but was also the firm in Grisham’s previous novels “The Associate” and “Gray Mountain”. Overall, “The Exchange” was another enjoyable fall outing with one of my favorite authors. For me, Grisham sets such a high bar for his readers that sometimes it’s hard to review his work with full objectively, since beauty is in the eyes of the beholder. I believe that that the key to Grisham’s continued success is his exemplary power to tell a captivating tale and this one was, although different in scope and focus, was still a strong and well-delivered read. See you again next year, my author friend and master storyteller… I can’t wait… And who knows if and when Mitch and Abby may show up again…

The Widow John Grisham As I have described in previous book reviews, it is time for one of my annual late Fall rituals. The leaves are falling (or if you are in Seattle, the rain is falling). College football is in full gear, racing towards the 12-team playoff, and the winter holidays are starting. It’s time to open the new John Grisham novel, “The Widow”, stay up way too late on two straight work nights, escaping into the legal world of thriller fiction. Although this one’s being promoted as Grisham’s first mystery novel, it is really a hybrid – what I will call a “legal mystery thriller”. This is the story of Simon Latch. He is not your typical John Grisham lead character that is being chased by bad guys while trying to fight an ethical battle. He is a flawed lawyer living in a small rural town in Virginia. He’s been in business for himself for over 18 years and the results are not good. He is just making just enough to pay bills thanks to some illegal sports gambling on the side. He loves his three children dearly, but the truth is he and his wife no longer like each other. Divorce is where they are headed, sooner than later. This is also the story of Eleanor Barnett, an 85-year-old widow who thinks that she just made a big mistake and needs Simon to make her a new will. Something seems off about her besides her frugal attitude and lack of trust. Somehow, she seems to be connecting with Simon, and according to her, nobody knows that her husband left her with a load of Coca-Cola and Walmart stock. She’s been able to hide these investments along with a large amount of cash from pretty much everyone, including friends and family. Her only concern is her husband’s two dead-beat sons from a previous marriage that she wants Simon to protect her estate from. Simon sees this incredible opportunity being handed to him and grabs it with both hands. He agrees to work hard to keep her wealth a secret and plots out an escape plan from his current wife and situation. However, things begin to happen that he can’t control. Eleanor has secrets and her behaviors keep pulling him in to take care of her growing needs. Before he knows it, she’s in a car accident that hospitalizes her and leads to him being arrested for a crime he cannot believe – that of murder! Simon knows that he is innocent, regardless of how bad the circumstantial evidence shows otherwise. With the entire town believing he killed someone and his family being forced to go into hiding, Simon has to find a killer before he spends the rest of his days in prison… After finishing “The Widow” I am a bit torn and conflicted. I am feeling well-spent yet also left frustrated. On one hand, it had a lot of the Grisham strengths that readers have come to expect and rely on from him. He is a masterful storyteller – smooth and fluid in his prose, engaging in his ability to capture the reader’s attention and emotional commitment, and once he has you, he never let’s go. You are along for the whole ride all the way to the end. I swear, he could write a cookbook and I would read it with enthusiasm that I didn’t know that I had. Yet, on the other hand, I also had some struggles with this one. I need to be careful not to give away any spoilers, so I am going to dance around the specifics a bit so as to not negatively impact someone else’s reading experience. For me, the first half of this book (200 pages) was a slow burn. A really slow burn that kept wondering when things were going to pick up. If it wasn’t for the book cover description that already told me what was coming, I would have had some serious moments of wondering what all of the work that Grisham was doing to set up his plotting what about. That does not mean that the first half wasn’t interesting, because it generally was. However, it involved a lot of time spent on introducing characters and setting up multiple storylines that would later come together and be needed in the second half. But truth be told, the slow burn didn’t provide the same level of danger and worry that usually comes with a Grisham legal thriller. More importantly, it just wasn’t as compelling as I was hoping for. Now that didn’t mean the payoff in the second half didn’t pay off on all of the build-up, because for the most part it did. Grisham connected most of the dots and brought an (albeit expected) emotional climax that left a poignant and indelible mark on this reader. However, at the same time, there were some pieces of the storylines that either were either dropped or felt a bit forced, but I won’t provide examples to avoid spoilers. Also, there was an important action taken by two of the characters that helped trigger and drive all of the second half conflict, but an explanation was never provided as to why they knew the information they had. Where or from who would they have received it. Certainly not from the killer. It was easy to ignore this plot point hole while reading the book (because Grisham is such an excellent storyteller), but after finishing the book, it kept coming back to me that this was a major plot point that just didn’t make sense. I apologize because this sound like an unfair teaser, but after reading the book, I think you will understand my point. The other thing that I wanted to mention is that Grisham used this story to make a point. One that you can tell is deeply important and personal to him. Because of that, he had to force the structure a bit to deliver the suffering emotional journey that Simon went through. For me, the court case decision didn’t align with the evidence, but that was part of the reality that Grisham wanted us to experience from the front seat. When you get to the end, everything he was trying to show came through brilliantly in the end. Grisham taught, pleaded, and preached on the unfortunate weaknesses that exist in our legal system. What I found really compelling on a personal level was that Simon was far from being a knight in shining armor. He didn’t help himself in several selfish and flawed ways and contributed to putting himself in a bad situation. But for me, that made his journey even stronger, because the cost was so high in many ways. As Grisham showed, the impact of legal outcomes affects so many more than just the one being charged and tried. In a nutshell, the last half of the book brought everything home (other than my constructive feedback listed above) and delivered the emotional impact and moral lesson that he intended. For me, that absolved most (but not quite all) of my critical comments. For me, I am going to error on the side of brevity and focus on what worked in this one, because what worked well made all of the difference for me.

The Widow is the best John Grisham novel that I've read in years. Grisham writes with an energetic and vibrancy that has been missing in his last batch of novels. ** spoiler alert ** Yeah, this is another stunner from Grisham. Just like a 69 yo man compared to a 32 yo man, this novel might lack the atomic bomb energy of “The Firm” or “The Client” or “The Runaway Jury”, but it sure as hell makes that up with its layers and profundity. Don’t get fooled by the lighthearted tone of the first part — after all, Grisham has always had a great sense of humor — and be ready to dive into a very serious topic that he is very passionate about. This topic is the miscarriage of justice, something that sadly still happens too often. Grisham has a long-standing and deep involvement with the Innocence Project, serving as a board member and ambassador for the organization. His activism began after researching his nonfiction book, "The Innocent Man," which tells the story of Innocence Project clients Ron Williamson and Dennis Fritz, who were exonerated after years of wrongful imprisonment. The Widow rotates around law and greed, classic Grisham. While some scenes are a bit slower than others, they are still important because without them, the court scenes wouldn’t be as masterful and mesmerizing as they are. By the end of this novel, you’ll be reflecting on how easy it is for a miscarriage of justice to take place, and about how extremely important the role of a juror is in our society. In fact, if you’re ever called to be a juror, that might as well be the greatest responsibility you’ll ever have in your life outside of your family. I’ve seen with my own eyes, as a juror myself about 8 years ago, some other jurors being blinded by ignorance, anger, personal issues, aggressively trying to go for a guilty verdict when there was not even a hint of a piece of evidence. Some of them were feeling vengeful because of the time that being on a jury was demanding out of their lives. That’s not the kind of people that you’re proud to have in your community. Luckily for the accused, the wiser minds prevailed that time. From an interview with the author: A: I had a big problem with the ending, which is unusual for me. I always know the ending before I start a book. I take a lot of time to outline the story and to really plot through the story before I start writing. I have these rules of writing proper fiction and that’s one: Do not write the first scene until you know the last scene. It was a unique experience for me. When I got to the end, I didn’t like it. My wife really didn’t like it. My agent, who is also my editor for 35 years, didn’t like it. So I said, “I’ll keep writing.” Now, the last quarter of the book is a whole new, major plot. ——— Read as audiobook, read by Michael Beck, who uses a convincing southern accent, although his pronunciation of “BECAUSE” made my ears bleed every time, as you can almost see the inflating of his cheeks like a puffer fish before making the letter “B” explode out like a petard.

Until he is accused of murder. This is a perfect blend of a legal thriller with a classic whodunit. The writing is superb and the character development was impressive. John Grisham definitely still has it. I will say the pacing felt a little inconsistent, slow in many parts and then a rapid fire race to the finish.

On a long road trip, my husband and I listened to the audible production of “A Gambling Man” by David Baldacci, narrated by Edoardo Ballerini and Brittany Pressley. The production of the novel is amazing. I think it’s Hachette Audio who did it. At any rate, Ballerini narrates most of the story except for the female voices. Pressley interjects her female parts throughout the story. Both Ballerini and Pressley provide an outstanding performance, providing imagination fodder for the listener. The story takes place in the late 1940’s, post WWII. The snappy dialogue involves the colloquialisms of the time. Women are “dames”, legs are “gams”, and the pace of the narration is in-line with the cadence of the time. I could picture Carole Lombard and Fred MacMurray as the main characters, Liberty Callahan and Alloysius Archer (aka Archer). The dialogues in this story are a joy to listen to. The story begins when Archer wins a 1939 Delahaye convertible in a card game in Reno. Archer plans to go to California where he can apprentice as a private Investigator. Archer picks up a dame, Liberty Callahan, who wants to leave Reno in pursuit of a Hollywood career. Of course, the couple run into trouble as they travel. When they get to California, Liberty immediately finds a job performing in a burlesque card club. Archer begins his apprenticeship with the legendary and former FBI agent Willie Dash. His first job is a blackmail scandal, which involves the main performer at the same burlesque club where Liberty works. Baldacci shines in his plot twists and turns. Dead bodies seem to turn up everywhere. Of course, there is a town “godfather” who is corrupt and runs the town. Archer is told by Willie Dash to “follow the money” and it leads Archer into some sticky situations. The story is great. It’s involved and full of unforeseen plot developments. What we enjoyed most though was the performance. The narration is pitch-perfect, catching the nuances of the time. I highly recommend the audio.

For the last couple of years, Baldacci has been producing two books a year, and focusing most of his attention on his series characters of Amos Decker (Memory Man), Will Robie, and John Puller. However, back in 2019, Baldacci introduced a new character – World War II veteran Aloysius Archer – in “One Good Deed” and opened readers up to a different historical era, that of post-war, 1949. I greatly enjoyed reading that change of pace set in the past, as well as Archer’s chivalrous character. Now, Baldacci has brought Archer back for his second outing – “A Gambling Man” and continuing his historical adventures into 1950. The book starts off with Archer, having left Poca City in his rearview mirror, making his way to California where he hopes to get a fresh start and start a new career. Thanks to his relationship with Detective Irving Shaw, Archer hopes to apprentice with Willie Dash, a former FBI agent and a successful private eye. On the way there, Archer gets off of the bus in Reno, Nevada, and the craziness begins. There he meets Liberty Callahan, a musical performer and actress, working her way to Hollywood. She leads him into a gambling win that adds to his stash, and a run-in with an older man ends up with Archer driving an extremely rare 1939 French Delahaye convertible. Getting himself out of Reno is not easy, and with Liberty as a traveling companion, they both hope for the best that California can offer. Upon arriving in the Southern coastal city of Baytown, Archer lands a job working for PI Dash as his apprentice, and on his first day they have a case thrown their way. Douglas Kemper, running for Mayor, has received a blackmail letter, threatening to expose an affair between him and Ruby Fraser, a young singer at the local adult club, Midnight Moods. Kemper insists there is no relationship and has no idea who could be coming after him, other than backers of his political opponent. Dash and Archer take the case and begin their investigation. They meet with Ruby and interview Kemper’s wife, whose father, Sawyer Armstrong, runs all of the major business in the city. Sawyer owns the key businesses in Baytown, including Midnight Moods, where Liberty is trying out as a fulltime singer. He controls the real estate, prostitution, gambling, and coastal sipping. And to make matters worse, Sawyer doesn’t like people talking with his daughter and sicks his two goons on Archer to let him know who’s running things. Then the investigation foes from political to deadly when someone is murdered and the stakes raised. Before he knows it, Archer finds himself in the middle of family issues, small town corruption, and deadly secrets that could very well cost him his life before his new career even gets started… There are a several good things to like about this book and Aloysius Archer. The first is Baldacci throwing himself into a historical time piece. It’s his own ode to Mickey Spillane and Dashel Hammett. The early 1950’s is far from today’s world full of technology, tools, and devices. It requires a strong ability to not only describe things like dress styles and transportation vehicles, but also truly understand the proper political and social norms, and enough details from post-World War II to provide the depth and quality needed to portray the true historical context. For example, Baldacci uses the social and legal inequality between men and women in that time period to propel and strengthen his story. My only criticism is that it seems every character in the book smokes constantly. I understand that smoking was a widespread social custom, but seriously, not every single person was a rabid smoker. Archer’s first book did a great job of introducing him and establishing his background. The problem was that it raised the bar and expectations for a second book. However, the good news is that this was almost as enjoyable a read as the first one. For the most part, Baldacci maintained the high level of quality throughout Archer’s second outing. His almost effortless, rhythmic writing style was there, stronger than ever. He connects his plot, characters, and style together like the lyrics of a good Eagles hit song that you just sing along with and get lost in the music. His books are a smooth and fluid read. There are no disruptions or hiccups in the flow of words. His language is descriptive, but focused on moving the story forward with mystery driven elements, action sequences and, moments of discovery along the way. Baldacci knows his characters and he shares them with us on an intimate level. As Archer works his way through the clues and deals with the obstacles thrown his way, important information is revealed step by step, like peeling away the layers of an onion. For an author that produces two books a year, Baldacci shows that he hasn’t lost his ability to create intricate plotting, character depth, and pacing. Overall, “A Gambling Man” is an enjoyable journey back in time when things were different and America was recovering and rebuilding following the devastation of World War II. For me, I consider this some of his most enjoyable work, reflecting fast-paced plotting, vigorous elements of mystery, and strong multi-dimensional characters you can appreciate. I am definitely interested in reading more Archer gumshoe adventures. Something tells me Baldacci feels the same way…

Video review coming soon... (my book tube channel) 'A Gambling Man' is David Baldacci's latest thriller. It stars Aloysius Archer - whom we last saw in 'One Good Deed'. Following the events in Poca City, Archer is on his way to California to see if a potential apprentice with a Private Detective will work out. He makes a stop in Reno, where after some action, he picks up a load of cash, a fancy automobile called a Delahaye and an aspiring actress named Liberty Callahan. Eventually, they reach Bay Town, California, a stopping point for would-be and failed stars. Archer gets the P.I. job and is immediately embroiled in a string of murders. I will be honest. Archer is the most forgettable Baldacci hero. Even Atlee Pine, with her set of ho-hum stories, is more memorable than Archer. I had to look up 'One Good Deed' to find out who Archer was and what he had done in his debut. I had given a high rating to that book which means that while the story is probably good, the lead character is quite bland. Essentially, I was starting 'A Gambling Man' without knowing who Archer was or why he was in Reno. 'A Gambling Man' is a slow burner and is unlike any other Baldacci I remember. The tone ranges from a noirish detective fiction like L.A. Confidential to an Alistair MacLean story like 'Fear is the Key'. I am not sure the cause and effect here, but the first half is a trudge. The third issue is that the author glosses over some plot points in the ending. We don't get to see some threads resolved while others are just papered over in the ' they lived happily ever after ' sort of way. Where the book does excel is in the detective work (mentioned earlier) as well as creating a 1950s kind of atmosphere. I like how Archer and his boss actually have to spend time going through books, records, legal records etc as well as canvas witnesses and informers. Archer, as such, is a decent character but I feel that Baldacci needs to add something extra to make him stand out. Overall, I liked 'A Gambling Man'. It will not figure in Baldacci's top 10, but neither is it bad. It is a flawed book that is entertaining once you get past the initial sections.

It was a book about books, it was a book about lovers. It was a book about books about lovers, it was a book about lovers of books. But above all, Book Lovers was a lovely book. Emily Henry really charms here. She knows her audience and delivers with grace, harnessing the aesthetics of book love amidst the sexual tension of two publishing professionals with a tendency for ferocity. As a fellow book lover, what really resonated was the way Henry captures the tendency to find narratives in the world around us, though for Nora this sef-type casting has allowed her public life as ‘the villain in someone else's love story,’ to rule her romantic life ‘because people like me don’t get those endings.’ With a keen eye for the classic elements of a romantic comedy, Book Lovers delightfully both subverts and satirizes tropes while simultaneously leaning into them in surprising ways that makes this story as humorously engaging as it is endlessly adorable. ‘Sometimes, even when you start with the last page and you think you know everything, a book finds a way to surprise you,’ Nora thinks, and this book captures that feeling so effortlessly. It’s the anti-Hallmark film Hallmark film narrative that acknowledges, sure, its fun to mock the stereotypical cliches and feel like you are above them, but you know deep down you still enjoy watching them even if you don’t care to admit it. Besides, who doesn’t want to save a small business while also falling in love!? Now sprinkle in all the book lover joys of small town indie bookstores, enemies-to-lovers coming together while editing a riveting novel, metaphors about not wanting to finish books and endlessly referencing favorite books to better explain a situation, and you’ll see why it is nearly impossible to not fall in love with Book Lovers. ‘She wonders whether what comes next could ever live up to the expectations. She doesn’t know. You never can. She turns the page anyway.’ Seriously though, I really loved this. It’s such a feel-good book that I simply could not put down. I love the aspect of the novel of all the juxtapositions of people and places with their fictional counterparts. The adorable small town of a novel is lackluster and lame, though maybe a place that can be beautiful if you give it enough time. Or the fictional Nora, Nadine Winters, that shows up in Dusty’s newest novel and forces Nora to confront her own public persona. I also loved the characters. Charlie is so wonderful and I adored his full commitment to Nora, smitten and supportive every step of the way. He could certainly charm the pants off me, watch out Nora. But she was delightful too. It’s so easy to fall in love with them both. And I gotta say, Charlie running and indie bookstore while having a full time job really hit deep. Representation matters, thanks Henry. I also loved the discussion on book endings, especially the ones that are ‘a reminder that there are things in life so valuable that you must risk the pain of losing them for the joy of briefly having them,’ which warmed my heart as a fan of messy or sad endings. Granted, this book does run a big long and the ending starts to drag but overall this book just made me happy. ‘ Maybe love shouldn’t be built on a foundation of compromises, but maybe it can’t exist without them either.’ While I found Happy Place a bit underwhelming, I found that all of the elements of this one worked really well. The banter is funny and adorable and I liked the calm pace that really let the scenes and characters breathe. The tension builds quite well and I enjoyed that Henry could discuss heavier themes amidst a rather sweet story as the slow understanding about Nora and her sister’s relationship was one of the most endearing aspects of the book. And not just the cutesy vacation checklist which leads to some good gaffs, but the tension between Libby wanting to he her own self and Nora wanting to always show she can support people and be reliable. I think what really makes this work is that there is more than just a romance going on—in fact Nora find the romance to be stressful because it distracts from her other problems. Like a good mixed drink, gotta add a some bitters to balance the sweetness. ‘I still feel like a city person, through and through, but maybe it’s possible to have more than one home. Maybe it’s possible to belong in a hundred different ways to a hundred different people and places.’ All in all, Book Lovers stole my heart. But how can it not when it so marvelously plays with the tropes of person and place aligning to make you swoon. Henry excels at giving a sense of place that draws you in and feels as much a character as those walking around it and here I found myself full up in this small town romance and everything that came with it. Because this book has a lot: publishing, small town charm while also embracing big city charm, hot guys, hot cousins of the hot guys, family drama, saving a small business, bad local theater, scandalous backstories, Bigfoot erotica, and did I mention hot guys? Book Lovers is a winner, and yes Emily Henry, ‘the romance gods would be proud.’ ⅘ ‘The last-page ache. The deep breath in after you’ve set the book aside.’

We've ALL seen that Hallmark movie (or at least part of it) featuring that hustle-and-bustle big city couple, where one half of the couple travels to the small town...and suddenly finds EVERYTHING they've been missing. The charm of a local yokel, with small town values and a bigger-than-the-sky heart sweeps in and shows them that the cold and callous big city and workaholic lifestyle just isn't what it's cracked up to be. The city slicker then comes to their senses, immediately breaking off the relationship with the seemingly callous and high-strung half of their relationship, and the NEW pairing live happily in small town bliss until the 'cows come home.' (Because there are probably cows, let's be real.) But what about the OTHER high-strung half of Couple A? What on EARTH happens to them? Such is the basis for Emily Henry's latest, Book Lovers. Nora is a literary agent by way of Miranda Priestley--the cold, Peloton-obsessed, workaholic Type A who is always the 'dumpee' in the aforementioned scenario. She's cycled through enough of these type of relationships to see the writing on the wall, but hasn't quite figured out how to break the spell. She forms an adversarial connection with Charlie Lastra, an editor, who just can't see the appeal of her client Dusty Fielding's latest, declaring it 'just isn't her best'. Nora feels she can both prove him wrong and keep a promise to her little sister Libby by taking a long trip to Sunshine Falls, North Carolina, where Dusty's latest takes place. She has a checklist of 'items' to complete, akin to the usual Hallmark movie plot points, to help her find love (well, she'll at least humor her sister.) But the LAST person she expects to see in this trip is the one man who can really make her blood boil: none other than Charlie Lastra himself. What on earth is he doing in THIS particular small town? What does this ugly twist of fate have in store for Nora...and is her little sister Libby hiding a big secret of her own? Will Nora find something buried deep within her that will have her questioning EVERYTHING? With no ability to 'flip to the last page' of her time in Sunshine Falls, will she follow her heart...no matter WHERE it leads? I've come to expect three things from Emily Henry's romances: 1) I'm going to laugh out loud, at least once. Probably many times. I'll also probably snort at least once and wish I could be 1/10th as witty as her characters. (Or just wish I could be friends with her characters...I'd settle for that!) 2) Her romances always have the same 'feel' without feeling repetitive. SUCH the sign of a good writer. You can pick up any of her books, and know it is irrefutably HERS. No over the top icky sexual scenes, just the perfect amount of spicy heat without being too graphic, and characters you want to see together so badly it HURTS by the time they actually do get together! 3) Deep emotional undertones and side plots that will catch you off guard. In this story, Nora's relationship with her sister really threw me for a loop and had me reflecting on my own life and relationship with my little sister. She dives right into these complicated relationships, giving them just as much weight and bearing as the main romantic relationship, and it helps to balance out her books. You know her characters as complete people, which is so important. Romantic relationships can be so fulfilling, but the most important relationship you will ever have is the relationship you have with yourself, and Henry never forgets that in her writing. Although her books never seem to grab me quite at a 5 star level, they're always SO close and as much as I anticipated this read, it lived up to every expectation. Emily Henry is just one of those writers who is like a cozy and familiar blanket you can snuggle with after a hard day and know she will provide you exactly the comfort and joy you need. (Even if it isn't Christmas time!) 🎄😉 4.5 shining stars! Nominated for Best Romance in the Goodreads Choice Awards!

“I can read you like a book.” 3.5 stars Book Lovers is an enemies to lovers romance about a literary agent and an editor whose mutual love of books draws them together. sake, and oh my god. it feels like two completely different people wrote book lovers and people we meet on vacation, maybe because henry wrote the latter during the height of a pandemic and the creative juices weren't all there given that we were, you know, battling a global disease. like.....not a single joke landed in people we meet on vacation. not one. just 300+ pages of no laughter. me reading people we meet on vacation: 😐😐😐😐😐😐😐😐😐😐🤨😐 me reading book lovers: 😂🤣😂😂😂😂🤣🤣🤣😂🤣😂😂 night and day. beyond the fact that i maintain alex/poppy had no real chemistry and just wanted to fuck really
