Now that my local library has restarted lending out book, I am catching up on my 2020 releases by James Patterson and his ever-growing stable of co-authors. This one - “The Summer House” - is Patterson’s annual summer read that is independent from his ongoing bestselling series. However, the complex story is more than what is advertised on the book jacket description and that turns out to be a good thing. In small-town, Sullivan Georgia, located near Savannah, is a dump of a Southern home that was once considered to be a luxurious summer getaway. It is now a rundown crash pad for a local drug dealer and users. It is here that a gruesome set of murders take place, including six adults and a two-year old girl. Local eyewitnesses reported to have seen to Army soldiers - a group of Rangers known as the Night Ninja’s – recently returned from Afghanistan and on leave from Army Hunter Airfield. The Army sends in major Jeremiah Cook and his Criminal Investigation Department (CID) team of four, including Agent Connie York, Captain Allen Pierce, Lt. John Huang, and Special Agent Manuel Sanchez. Cook is a war veteran and former NYPD cop who suffers daily from a serious leg injury suffered when his Humvee was struck by an IED in Afghanistan. York is his second-in-command; Pierce is the JAG lawyer; Huang is the psychiatrist, and Sanchez is an investigator. However, Cook and his investigative team are in way over their heads in what appears to be a clear and cut case with the killers already in custody. In addition, they are not received well by either local law enforcement nor the Army officials at Hunter Airfield. Both the Sherriff’s department and military leaders refuse to provide any help, challenge their every move, and stonewall any opportunity to question witnesses. The more Cook’s team digs into the damning evidence, they find that the pieces just don’t all seem to fit together as well as they are being presented. Things don’t make sense and the investigators are starting to sense there are secrets behind the arrest of the Rangers that are more than what is being stated publicly. Then things take an ugly turn when the team members start being followed, attacked, and then told to leave. In order to uncover the truth, Cook and his team will need to risk not only their careers, but also their own lives… The good news is this is a good suspenseful read. It is markedly better than the average Patterson novel. It was fresh in its delivery, maximizing a uniquely multi-layered cast throughout the story. Each member of the investigative team was patriotic, well intentioned, yet flawed individuals who make mistakes trying to do the right thing. Their professional and personal struggles blended in well with Cook’s own war demons, and their mission to seek justice. One of the major strengths was the multi-layered plot that was well developed, mixing both investigative mystery elements with dramatic action sequences into a tense and thoroughly enjoyable reading experience. The characters, plotting, and locations all blended together effectively. It was definitely a nice change for a summer read. The only complaint that I have is that I felt the climax could have included a bit more payoff. Don’t get me wrong, the build-up to the climax was strong. It’s just that the payoff itself was briefer than I expected. I wanted more physical retribution in the finale, more emotional closure after reading 400 plus pages. This may be a small nit on my part that others may not experience, but I think it is worthy enough to mention. Still, it did not take away much from a good read. Overall, “The Summer House” reminded me a bit of the NCIS television show and Nelson DeMille’s 2001 novel “The General’s Daughter”, but not in a bad way. It was strong mind-candy that served its entertaining purpose well.

The only problem is Oswald is also a psychopath, who is on a revenge mission on another group of hackers. That small group managed to hack into Oswald’s network that caused him great financial loss. Now Oswald is killing them one by one and neither the Police nor Stephanie can lay their hands on him. This is the most light-heartedly written serious thriller, where Stephanie’s grandma, Mazur, provides the comic relief and with great panache! When Stephanie rescues one of Oswald’s target hackers and provides him shelter at her paternal house, grandma Mazur takes him under her wings and becomes his self-announced assistant and mentor both! The big question is can Stephanie keep Oswald away from them and nab him before he kills someone else, or will this be the end of the hackers’ group – Baked Potatoes? Read more to find out! Can they find him before more people are killed and he is able to launch a plot with international repercussions? Game On: Tempting Twenty-Eight reminded me that maybe the series isn’t complete until I read the “tweeners.” There are a few books in between the numbers that I kinda sorta skipped. That’s where you’ll find Diesel, a mysterious, dangerous spy (of sorts) with a penchant for sleeping in Steph’s bed sans pajamas. I don’t think this novel does him justice, because I didn’t think his role here was all that impressive. He gets more and more helpful and daring as the book goes on, however. I had that scary/thrilled moment again when Steph gets…in trouble (no spoilers). I have to say I have a love-hate relationship with Steph’s competence. She’s getting more and more able, although she needs to call Ranger or Morelli (and now Diesel) for help. And yes, she ends up with whipped cream or guacamole or beaver guts all over her after some disaster or another, and yes…she blows up a car. Or cars. But it seems the days of total bumbling and slapstick humor are drifting away. I don’t know: I kinda miss the goofy Steph. But I also like this one: she’s both tough AND smart, and a little more careful. What do you think? Summer task: read 29 and 30, in anticipation of Now or Never, coming out in November!

Because I'm a loser, I had never read Janet Evanovich until this summer when I read the last book in another one of her series. So, in keeping with tradition I'm starting, what I hear is her most popular series, at the very end. Game On is the 28th(!) book in her Stephanie Plum series and it's easy to see why Plum has such longevity. I had no idea what to expect but I assure you it wasn't what I just read. I'm not sure I've laughed as much reading as I did with Game On. It was a total delight. The story was a good cat-and-mouse thriller with a sadistic computer hacker but the real star of the show are the characters. Especially Plum's grandma. My grandmother is a horrible human being, so I long for a grandma like Plum's who is hilarious and loves life. All the characters are unique, quirky and compliment each other. They are all dysfunctional in the best way and really propel the story in the down times. Needless to say, Mrs. Evanovich has gained a new fan. Better late than never. My thanks to Mrs. Evanovich, Atria Books, and NetGalley for the privilege of reading an advance copy of Game On.

After the debacle of Box 9 I needed something light and easy to read to clear my mind. This fit the bill perfectly. Stephanie, Diesel and the gang go after a crazed and murderous hacker in this one. Not as hilariously funny as some of the previous books, but it was just what I needed. I have read every book in this series and liked them all, except for the one about the zombies, but I have forgiven Evanovich for that misfire. Recommended to anyone with a sense of humor.

This is one series, where you have to admire Janet Evanovich with her stamina to keep going and writing each book, to be honest, I thought after reading 27 and being a little disappointed with it, that I wouldn't enjoy 28 as much but she made this one an action-packed novel with the arrival of Diesel and Wulf. Part of me keeps thinking, how long can she keep this up and when the hell are we getting a finale with Stephanie and Joe Morelli but the other part is still enjoying the various scenarios that Stephanie and her family keep getting into. I liked this one as we saw a bit more interaction between Stephanie's dad and Mother as they open their home as a safe place for two of the "Baked Potatoes" - a hacking group, that Stephanie is trying to protect. In Game On we see Stephanie's main target is a high profile hacker named Oswald Wednesday who loves to torture and keep everyone on their toes, he also loves to blow things up which for Stephanie means this time around- she isn't the only one whose vehicles get blown up as Diesel will lose a motorhome and a motorbike. Diesel and Wulf feature in Game On as their boss "Auntie" has been hired to track down Oswald and so Diesel will pair up with Stephanie and of course, Lula to find Oswald. In Game On, we also have a small part with the handsome Ranger and it also acts as a bit of a prequel to a new series called The Recovery Agent as another bondswoman Gabriella Rosa is mentioned. On the Joe Frontier - the idea of marriage is floating around but it looks like the pair love their casual relationship and no hints of wedding bells shortly. As I finish Book #28, it does make me realize I have been reading this series now for 11 years as I decided at the end of 2011 to make it my goal to read the Stephanie Plum series starting with Book #1, and here I am now 11 years later reading Book #28. I wonder if Janet's lucky number to end this series will be #30? Who Knows? All, I can say is that this was another action-packed, LOL, car-bombing, love triangle Stephanie Plum novel and I look forward to more adventures from this Trenton bounty hunter and her fun-loving sidekicks of Lula and Grandma Mazur.

I don't read these because I am expecting great literature or a thriller with tons of twists and turns. I have been reading the series for so long that I am entertained by Stephanie and Lula getting up to the same hijinks. This is better than the last few. Diesel makes an appearance hunting for the same guy that Stephanie is. Lula gets shot which makes things more real. Stephanie loses multiple cars and Ranger has some help coming to the rescue.

For light relief, the Stephanie Plum series by Janet Evanovich is hard to beat. I hadn’t realised I’d missed quite so many instalments until I looked it up but luckily, even though I’ve skipped from #18 to #28, it makes little difference. In Game On, bond enforcement agent, Stephanie, with the assistance of an astrological challenged Lula, is chasing five FTA’s- a homeless man who roasts ducks in a local park, an exhausted mother who shot up a bakery when all she wanted was an eclair, a man who makes his living as an event ‘mooner’, a computer hacker who replaced the evening news with a porno clip, and international cyber criminal and murderous psychopath, Oswald Wednesday, who is way out of Stephanie’s league. Luckily Diesel, who is also after Wednesday on behalf of his mysterious employer, and Ranger, are around to back Stephanie up, which is convenient when she has a source she needs to protect, yet another car meets an untimely demise, and she and Lula are taken hostage. There’s a formula to the Stephanie Plum series that involves bad luck, disaster and near misses, offset by wisecracks, healthy dose of slapstick, and sexual tension, so there aren’t any surprises in the plot of Game On exactly, but it is fast paced and entertaining. I always enjoy Lula’s antics, giggle at Grandma Mazur’s sass, and lust after Ranger, Morelli, (and now Diesel too), as Stephanie barely manages to keep it together. Game On is another fun instalment in the Stephanie Plum series, I expect fans will enjoy this, as should first timers.

Frankly, it’s time for Janet to end this series. Looks like a new series is coming out shortly. This just lacked the fun and craziness of previous novels. Lula had most of the bad stuff happen to her. I still am invested in this author and the light tone of her stories.
